title: IELTS Academic Practice 01 · Original set
description: Original Academic practice: 40 Listening questions, 40 Reading questions and two Writing tasks. Recordings use synthetic voices. Scores are practice estimates; Writing requires rubric-based review. Speaking is practised separately.

parts.transcript:
Receptionist: Good morning, Riverside University Residences. How can I help?

Maya: Hello. My name is Maya Patel. That's P A T E L. I'm coming for a short research course in October, and I'd like to ask about accommodation.

Receptionist: Certainly. We have rooms in North Court and a few in the older South House. What dates are you considering?

Maya: I originally wrote down the 12th, but the course now starts on the 14th, so I'd need to arrive on Monday the 13th of October.

Receptionist: And how long would you stay?

Maya: Eight nights. I leave on the Tuesday morning after the course.

Receptionist: That's fine. We offer single rooms, twin rooms and a small number of studios. The studios have their own kitchenette, but they're more expensive.

Maya: A single room should be enough. I won't be cooking much.

Receptionist: I'll note that. Single rooms are on the third floor of North Court. There is a lift, so the stairs aren't essential.

Maya: That sounds suitable. Is there a deposit?

Receptionist: Yes, it's 80 pounds, payable by card when we confirm the booking. It's returned after a room inspection, provided there's no damage.

Maya: All right. Where do I collect the key? I'll probably arrive after the office closes.

Receptionist: The main office closes at six, but late arrivals collect keys from the security desk beside the main gate. You'll need photo identification.

Maya: Does the price include breakfast?

Receptionist: It does. The dining room opens at 7:15 on weekdays and half an hour later on Sundays. A packed breakfast can be arranged if you have an early departure.

Maya: I'll probably have one early morning. Is there somewhere to store a suitcase after check-out?

Receptionist: Yes, guests can leave luggage in the locked room beside reception until five o'clock. Please keep valuables with you; the residence is not responsible for items left in luggage. There is also a small common room with a kettle, but cooking is not permitted in bedrooms.

Maya: I'm attending a course in the science building. Is North Court far from it?

Receptionist: About ten minutes on foot. The quickest route crosses the central quad. If you arrive after dark, use the lit path along the library rather than the shortcut behind the sports hall.

Maya: I may need that once. One other thing: could the room be away from the laundry room? I'm a light sleeper, and machines at night might be a problem.

Receptionist: I can request that. I can't guarantee a particular room, but I'll put it on the booking.

Maya: Thank you.

Receptionist: Finally, your reference is N as in November, followed by 6042. I'll email the confirmation in a few minutes.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.instructions: Play the synthetic recording once. Read the question limits carefully before you begin.
parts.transcript:
Welcome to the Greenway Museum. Before you begin, I'll explain a few changes to the visitor programme. The museum used to close at four on weekdays, but many local visitors said they could not arrive before finishing work. We now remain open until seven on Thursdays, when the final admission is at half past six. This is not a late opening every day, and it was not introduced to cut weekend staffing.

For families, the standard ticket includes access to all permanent galleries and a printed map. The craft table is available at weekends for a small additional charge, while guided tours must be booked separately. Our popular rooftop walk is limited to twelve people because of the narrow stairway, so please reserve a place even if you have already bought a ticket. It is usually held in light rain; it is not automatically cancelled simply because the weather is poor.

The café in the west corridor is closed for the moment. The museum has not changed its catering company; the kitchen is being redesigned to improve ventilation. A drinks cart is operating in the courtyard, and the café is expected to reopen in late November.

If you only have an hour, I suggest the audio guide. It selects eight key objects and takes about forty-five minutes. It is not specifically a children's service, and all the labels are available in large print. The guide is useful for visitors who want a clear route through the building without stopping at every display.

The building itself has a complicated history. The East Gallery was once a warehouse, and some of the original loading doors are still visible behind the modern display cases. The museum keeps them exposed because they show how large objects entered the building. In contrast, the Archive Wing was added in the 1980s and has stricter light and humidity controls.

Visitors who need step-free access should use the side entrance beside the courtyard. The main entrance has three steps, although staff can provide a portable ramp. Wheelchairs are available without charge, but they cannot be reserved online. Photography is permitted in the permanent galleries without flash; temporary exhibitions may have different rules.

Now, a quick orientation. The East Gallery contains the museum's industrial collection, including the original weaving machinery. If you are interested in contemporary work, look in the courtyard, where temporary installations are changed every few months. The Archive Wing is at the rear. It has a quiet reading area for researchers, although visitors must ask the attendant before consulting documents.

The oldest surviving wall is not in the Archive Wing. It runs along the northern edge of the courtyard and formed part of the town's first market hall. Finally, printing demonstrations take place in the East Gallery on the first Saturday of each month, beside the reconstructed press.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.instructions: Play the synthetic recording once. Read the question limits carefully before you begin.
parts.transcript:
Tutor: So, let's look at your project on public libraries and social participation. I see that your question has changed.

Zoe: Yes. At first we asked whether libraries increase community involvement across the whole city, but that was too broad. We couldn't get consistent information from every district.

Liam: And another group had already studied city-wide volunteering, so we narrowed it to how library programmes affect people's use of local spaces.

Tutor: That makes sense. How have you defined a regular library user?

Zoe: Someone who comes at least once a week.

Tutor: That might exclude people who use the library online or attend a monthly workshop. I suggest you use a broader definition: anyone who has used at least two library services in the past three months. State that clearly in the method section.

Liam: We've drafted a questionnaire. It asks people to rate the library and then describe what they do in the neighbourhood.

Tutor: I noticed the opening sentence says, "How has the library improved your community life?" That assumes improvement has occurred. The introduction sounds biased. Ask a neutral question first, such as "What effect, if any, has the library had?"

Zoe: Should we distribute it only inside libraries?

Tutor: No. That would miss people who stopped attending. Use two libraries, a community centre and an online link. You will still have a convenience sample, but at least it will not be drawn from one building.

Liam: We're comparing the libraries by computer numbers, opening hours and activity programmes.

Tutor: Computer numbers are easy to count, but the activity programme is probably more relevant to your question. Public transport is worth recording as context, not as a main comparison. Focus on the range of activities and how users describe them.

Zoe: One result surprised us. People who attended language exchanges were more likely to report visiting parks and markets, although they may already have been unusually active.

Liam: I thought that was quite significant. It suggests the library is acting as a gateway to the neighbourhood.

Tutor: Perhaps, but language-exchange participants may already be unusually active or new to the area. The association may be caused by an unexamined factor, such as length of residence. You should not claim a direct effect.

Zoe: We'll explain that limitation. We have twelve slides, but some contain large tables.

Liam: Our sources are mostly questionnaire responses, but we also made notes during two library events.

Tutor: Keep those observation notes separate from the questionnaire data. They can illustrate what happened at the events, but they were not collected using the same method. In the presentation, label them as field observations and avoid combining their numbers with the survey results.

Zoe: We have a spreadsheet showing responses by age group, but the youngest group is very small.

Tutor: Then show the size of each group as well as the percentages. A percentage based on twelve people can look more certain than it is. You may keep the age comparison descriptive, but do not imply that the groups are statistically equivalent.

Liam: Would a quotation from one participant help?

Tutor: Yes, if it is anonymised and clearly presented as an illustration rather than representative evidence. One person's comment can explain a pattern, but it cannot establish how common the experience is.

Tutor: Put the detailed figures in an appendix. On the slides, show one clear chart and describe the pattern verbally. Also explain the sample limitation; an audience trusts results more when the boundaries are visible.

Liam: We present next Wednesday, don't we?

Tutor: It was moved. You are now scheduled for Thursday afternoon, at two o'clock.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.instructions: Play the synthetic recording once. Read the question limits carefully before you begin.
parts.transcript:
Today's lecture considers urban wetlands as flood-management infrastructure. A wetland is not simply a pond with reeds. It is a shallow, periodically wet system in which soil, plants and water interact. The first mechanism is physical: water entering a wetland spreads across a rough surface, so its movement slows. In technical terms, the wetland increases surface roughness. That delay can reduce the height of a flood peak downstream.

Vegetation contributes in several ways. Stems and leaves obstruct flow, while roots hold soil in place. They also trap floating debris, which otherwise might block a culvert. A wetland basin may fill quickly during a storm, but it releases water gradually through soil infiltration and controlled outlets. Its value therefore depends on the whole sequence, not on the depth of water at one moment.

Historically, many cities drained wetlands. Engineers associated them with stagnant water, disease and difficult construction. Property developers also considered them unproductive land. These assumptions were not entirely irrational in crowded nineteenth-century districts, but they led to the loss of natural storage. Modern projects are now restoring shallow basins beside streams and transport corridors.

Restoration is not a matter of digging a hole and adding attractive plants. The site must connect to the wider catchment, so that water can enter and leave at appropriate rates. A sealed ornamental pond may look wet but contribute little to flood control. The strongest designs include open pools, muddy shelves and dense vegetation. This mixture creates different flow paths and habitats. The flood benefit is generally greatest when open water and vegetation are both present.

Poor design creates new problems. If an inlet is too narrow, fast water can scour one bank and deposit sediment in an unintended area. If the outlet is too high, the basin may remain permanently flooded, killing plants adapted to periodic drying. Designers should also consider mosquitoes, public access and the safety of children, rather than treating ecology and people as separate issues.

Wetlands can improve water quality as well as reduce flood peaks. Sediment settles in slow water, and plant roots can take up some nutrients. This service has limits. A wetland overloaded by road salt or industrial pollutants may store contamination rather than remove it, and the material may later enter the food chain. Monitoring should therefore include chemical indicators as well as water level.

Maintenance is often underestimated. Invasive plants may crowd out the species that provide the best habitat, while litter can block an inlet. Some projects use seasonal mowing or controlled removal, but excessive disturbance can destroy nesting sites. Managers need a schedule that reflects the wetland's hydrology instead of treating it like an ordinary lawn.

How do we know whether a project works? Photographs are useful for communication, and one measurement after a dramatic storm can reveal an important event, but neither is enough for comparison. Researchers usually measure water levels at the inlet and outlet, record rainfall, and repeat the observations across several seasons. Seasonal records capture dry periods, ordinary storms and exceptional events. They also reveal whether a wetland is gradually filling with sediment.

The main conclusion is conceptual. Urban wetlands should not be regarded as decorative landscaping that happens to be wet. They are a form of infrastructure: they store, slow and filter water. At the same time, they provide habitat, shade and opportunities for environmental education. Their ecological benefits do not replace careful engineering, but they make the investment perform more than one public function.

modules.title: Reading

parts.title: Passage 1
parts.passage:
[1] For much of the twentieth century, tidal energy was associated with barrages: enormous walls built across estuaries to trap seawater and release it through turbines. A barrage can generate substantial electricity, but it also changes the movement of sediment, fish and boats. In the last two decades, engineers have therefore renewed interest in a less conspicuous technology: tidal-stream turbines. These machines resemble underwater wind turbines and are placed where currents are strong enough to turn their blades.

[2] The attraction of a tidal stream is predictability. Wind and sunlight fluctuate from hour to hour, whereas the timing of a tide can be calculated years in advance. Predictability does not mean constant output. A turbine produces little during slack water, when the tide changes direction, and its output depends on the speed of the current. Nevertheless, electricity planners can anticipate the broad pattern and combine several sites with other renewable sources.

[3] The first design challenge is the marine environment. Salt water corrodes metal, waves exert forces that are difficult to reproduce in a laboratory, and maintenance vessels cannot always reach a machine when its blades need attention. Designers have experimented with protective coatings, sealed generators and platforms that can be raised above the surface. A device that is slightly less efficient but easy to retrieve may produce more electricity over its lifetime than a high-performing device that spends months awaiting repair.

[4] Environmental assessment is equally important. A slowly turning blade is not automatically harmless to marine animals. The risk depends on blade speed, visibility, the species present and the alternative routes available to fish and mammals. Monitoring therefore combines underwater cameras, acoustic instruments and observations by local fishermen. Early projects sometimes promised a simple answer-either "no impact" or "unacceptable impact"-but contemporary studies tend to measure particular risks under particular conditions.

[5] Sediment is another concern. A turbine extracts energy from moving water, and a group of turbines may slightly alter local currents. The change could affect mudflats or the distribution of nutrients, although the size and direction of the effect vary by site. Baseline surveys before construction are essential. Without them, a later change may be blamed on the turbines when it is actually part of a natural cycle.

[6] Public acceptance can decide a project long before construction begins. Coastal communities may support low-carbon electricity but object to restrictions on fishing or navigation. Developers have found that early meetings work better when maps show possible exclusion zones and when fishermen are invited to contribute observations. Compensation alone is not always persuasive; people also want confidence that the project's benefits will remain local.

[7] The location of a turbine is consequently a compromise between physics and access. The strongest current may lie in a channel used by ferries, while a slightly weaker site may be easier to connect to the electricity network. Engineers model the seabed, but local boat operators often know where anchoring is safe, where sand shifts after storms and when visibility becomes dangerous. Including that knowledge can improve the design even when it changes the preferred site. It can also reveal seasonal conflicts that a short technical survey would miss.

[8] Planning authorities increasingly ask developers to distinguish construction effects from operating effects. Installing a foundation may disturb sediment for a few weeks, whereas a rotating device may alter animal movement for years. Neither type of impact should be treated as automatically decisive. The useful question is whether the effect is measurable, reversible and acceptable in relation to the energy and employment a project provides. This approach makes monitoring a condition of permission rather than a public-relations exercise completed before construction.

[9] Costs remain high because the industry lacks the manufacturing scale enjoyed by wind power. Each marine site has different seabed conditions, current speeds and grid connections. Standardization is difficult, yet some components-power cables, monitoring equipment and maintenance procedures-can be shared. A likely future is not a single universal turbine but a family of designs adapted from common engineering principles.

[10] The most realistic view of tidal power is therefore neither exuberant nor dismissive. It will not replace every fossil-fuel station, and it cannot provide electricity at exactly the moment consumers request it. It can, however, add a predictable stream of renewable generation in places where the environmental and social costs are acceptable. The success of a project will be judged not merely by the energy captured below the water, but by how carefully the whole coastal system is understood.

[11] Grid planners must also consider the timing of maintenance. If several devices in a small region require servicing during the same period of weak tides, the expected output may fall together. Forecasting tools can help schedule work, but they cannot remove the logistical difficulty of moving crews and equipment at sea. A mature industry would need shared ports, trained technicians and emergency plans as well as better turbines.

[12] The financial model reflects these uncertainties. Investors may want a long contract before paying for equipment, while regulators may prefer a small trial until ecological evidence is stronger. Staged development can bridge the gap: a few machines are installed, their effects and reliability are monitored, and later expansion depends on the results. This is slower than announcing a large project, but it reduces the chance that a promising technology is judged by one poorly managed site.

parts.title: Passage 2
parts.passage:
[1] The modern repair café began with a practical question: what would happen if people were given a place, tools and company in which to repair broken household objects? The answer, in many towns, has been a recurring event staffed by volunteers who fix lamps, clothing, small appliances and bicycles. The movement is sometimes described as a response to consumer waste, but its organizers usually make a broader claim. Repair cafés can change people's relationship with objects by making the hidden work of maintenance visible.

[2] The word "café" is significant. Most events offer tea or another simple refreshment, and visitors sit beside volunteers rather than handing an object over at a commercial counter. This arrangement creates an educational exchange. A volunteer may replace a switch, but will often explain why the old one failed and how to recognize the warning signs next time. The visitor is not merely a customer receiving a service; ideally, the visitor becomes more capable.

[3] That ideal is not always reached. Some objects arrive with faults that are unsafe to investigate, while others require proprietary parts or software. Volunteers must know when to stop. A successful repair is not measured by the number of objects opened, but by whether the process is safe and whether the owner understands the likely outcome. Organizers commonly use disclaimers, yet a disclaimer cannot substitute for careful judgement.

[4] The environmental case for repair is complicated. Extending the life of a kettle avoids the materials and energy associated with manufacturing a replacement, but transporting a volunteer across town or buying an unusual spare part also has a footprint. More importantly, not every repair prevents a purchase. Some owners keep the repaired object as a spare and buy a new one anyway. Researchers therefore distinguish between the technical life of an object and its service life in a household.

[5] Repair cafés also reveal the social geography of waste. Events are often most popular in neighbourhoods where residents already possess tools, time and confidence. People on lower incomes may have more to gain from repair but less flexibility to attend a Saturday afternoon event. Some organizers have responded by holding sessions in housing estates, libraries and schools, or by offering evening appointments. Accessibility is treated as a design problem rather than as evidence that a community is uninterested.

[6] The movement has influenced policy discussions about the "right to repair." Campaigners argue that manufacturers should provide spare parts, repair manuals and software access for a reasonable period. Producers respond that uncontrolled repair can compromise safety, cybersecurity or brand reputation. The dispute is not simply between environmentalists and businesses. Some manufacturers now offer modular products because repairability can reduce warranty costs and appeal to consumers, while others say that a modular design may use more material at the outset.

[7] Measurement is difficult. Counting repaired objects is easy, but it does not tell us whether the event changed future purchasing. Surveys can ask about intentions, although people do not always behave as they predict. A more informative evaluation may combine attendance records, follow-up interviews, the age of repaired products and local waste data. Even then, the results will be shaped by the event's location and the kinds of objects volunteers are prepared to handle.

[8] The repair café is consequently neither a complete solution to waste nor a symbolic gesture with no practical effect. Its strongest contribution may be cultural. It interrupts the assumption that a broken object has already become rubbish and gives people a vocabulary for discussing durability, design and responsibility. The number of objects rescued matters, but so does the number of people who begin to ask whether replacement was necessary in the first place.

[9] This cultural effect can influence markets indirectly. If customers begin asking for replaceable batteries or accessible spare parts, retailers may pass the request to manufacturers. A single event will not change a supply chain, but a network of events can make repeated failures visible across towns. Repairers sometimes share anonymized records of faults, creating a form of public evidence that sits between a personal anecdote and a formal product audit.

[10] The movement has also encouraged a more precise conversation about design. Volunteers notice recurring failures: glued cases that cannot be opened, batteries that are sealed inside a product and software that refuses to run after a minor component is replaced. These observations can be reported to manufacturers and regulators, although a repair café is not a laboratory with a representative sample. Its evidence is especially useful for identifying practical frustrations that formal product testing may overlook.

[11] There is a financial question as well. A volunteer event can offer help at little direct cost, but it still depends on donated space, insurance, tools and coordination. If organizers become responsible for repairing every object in a neighbourhood, the informal model may collapse. Some cafés therefore train new volunteers, publish lists of professional services and concentrate on teaching rather than promising that every item will be saved. Boundaries protect both safety and trust.

[12] In this sense, repair is partly an educational relationship. A visitor who learns to replace a cable may later choose a durable product, keep spare parts or ask a retailer about repairability. Such changes are difficult to attribute to one event, but they are consistent with the movement's larger ambition: to make the life of an object visible before a purchase and after a fault.

parts.title: Passage 3
parts.passage:
[1] For most of human history, the night sky was a common visual environment. People navigated by stars, marked seasons by constellations and told stories in which celestial objects acted as calendars, ancestors or warnings. Artificial light has not erased those uses everywhere, but it has transformed the conditions under which urban populations encounter the sky. The modern debate about light pollution is therefore not only a technical argument about energy. It is also a dispute about access to a shared cultural landscape.

[2] The phrase "light pollution" covers several phenomena. Skyglow is the bright dome above a city, produced when upward or reflected light scatters in the atmosphere. Glare reduces visibility because a bright source lies within the observer's field of view. Light trespass occurs when illumination crosses a boundary-for example, a security lamp shining into a bedroom. Unlike a single smokestack, these effects are distributed across streets, buildings, advertisements and vehicles. Their sources may be individually small while their combined influence is extensive.

[3] Astronomers have obvious reasons to be concerned. Faint stars disappear against a bright background, and long-exposure images become more difficult. Yet scientific observatories are not the only stakeholders. Many nocturnal animals use darkness to forage, migrate or avoid predators. Insects are drawn towards some lights, bats may change their routes, and sea turtle hatchlings can move inland rather than towards the reflection of the ocean. Human health research is examining whether excessive night-time light affects sleep, although the strength and meaning of the evidence vary by exposure and individual.

[4] The first policy response in many cities was to replace old street lamps with more efficient sources. This can reduce electricity use, but efficiency does not automatically reduce skyglow. A brighter lamp may consume less energy per unit of illumination while increasing total light. The relevant question is not simply how efficient a lamp is, but whether the right amount of light reaches the right place at the right time. Shielding, dimming and warmer colour temperatures can be as important as the lamp's rated efficiency.

[5] Some residents resist reductions in lighting because they associate brightness with safety. The relationship is not straightforward. A very bright source can create deep shadows beyond its pool of light, while uniform, carefully directed illumination may make movement easier to see. Crime statistics are affected by many variables, so a change in lighting cannot be evaluated by intuition alone. Public consultation is particularly important when a proposed reduction affects routes used by pedestrians, shift workers or people with visual impairments.

[6] The sky is also becoming an arena for commercial activity beyond the atmosphere. Large satellite constellations can provide communication services, but their reflective surfaces may create bright moving points that interfere with astronomical observations and alter the appearance of the night sky. Supporters emphasize connectivity and emergency communication; critics ask whether orbital operations should be governed by a stronger public-interest standard. The disagreement echoes the terrestrial debate: benefits are widely distributed, while unwanted effects may be experienced by particular communities.

[7] Several cities have introduced "dark-sky" zones, especially near observatories, wetlands or parks. Such zones do not necessarily demand complete darkness. They may restrict advertising, require shielding or set curfews for decorative lighting. Their success depends on enforcement and on whether neighbouring districts simply send light across the boundary. A zone is therefore better understood as part of a regional plan than as an isolated patch of darkness.

[8] Measurement helps a city decide whether a lighting change has worked. Photometers can record sky brightness, while satellite observations reveal broad patterns of upward light. Neither method captures the whole experience. A sensor may show improvement above a park while a poorly aimed lamp still creates glare at eye level. Residents' reports, wildlife surveys and observations from amateur astronomers can add detail, provided that the data are collected at comparable times and locations.

[9] Colour also matters, though it is not a magic solution. Shorter-wavelength light scatters more strongly in the atmosphere and may affect some animals differently from warmer light. A warm lamp that is too bright can still produce pollution, while a dimmer, well-shielded source may be less disruptive even if its colour is not ideal. Policy should therefore avoid turning one product feature into a universal answer.

[10] Governance is complicated because lighting is controlled by many owners. A municipality may manage street lamps, private businesses may illuminate façades and households may install security lights. A successful programme needs common standards, clear responsibility and a way for residents to report problems. It may also need to explain that darkness is not an absence of public care: in some places, reducing glare makes the existing light more useful.

[11] The debate is likely to continue as cities become denser and more connected. A district may advertise its dark sky as a cultural attraction while another district argues that brightly lit signs support local businesses. Neither claim can be settled by a universal brightness target. The practical task is to make trade-offs explicit, collect evidence after changes are introduced and leave room for the policy to be revised when people, animals or technologies respond in unexpected ways.

[12] There is no single ideal level of illumination. A hospital entrance, a rural wildlife corridor and a sports stadium have different needs. The challenge is to replace the crude assumption that more light is always better with a more precise conversation about purpose, timing and consequence. If the night sky is treated as a shared environment, decisions about light must account for people who look through telescopes, people who sleep beside a lamp, animals that travel after sunset and future generations who may otherwise inherit a permanently bright horizon.

parts.transcript:
Coordinator: Good afternoon, Westfield Community Garden. Are you calling about volunteering?

Noah: Yes. I've just moved nearby and would like to join. My surname is Hassan-H-A-S-S-A-N.

Coordinator: Welcome, Noah. The garden is behind the old fire station on Mill Road. We have an orientation for new members on Saturday 6 June.

Noah: I'm away that Saturday. Is there another one?

Coordinator: The next session is Tuesday 9 June at six in the evening. I'll put you down for that. Membership is 25 pounds a year, which covers insurance and seeds.

Noah: That's reasonable. Do I need to bring equipment?

Coordinator: We provide large tools, but everyone should bring their own gloves. The shed opens at eight on work mornings. Please don't arrive earlier, because the alarm is still active.

Noah: How much produce can members take?

Coordinator: Usually one basket of vegetables each week. It varies with the harvest, and the rule is more generous in summer than in winter.

Noah: I've grown tomatoes before. Is there training?

Coordinator: Yes. The compost course is in August, and there's a short session on seed saving in September.

Noah: Great. I'd like to help with tomatoes, especially.

Coordinator: I'll note that. Our emergency number is 01944 31872. Only use it for an accident or a serious security problem.

Noah: How are new members assigned to a plot? I don't want to take over a bed someone else is using.

Coordinator: We have shared beds rather than private plots. The weekly rota is on the noticeboard, and a team leader shows you where to work at your first session. Please label anything you bring, because tools and seed trays are often similar. If you cannot attend your assigned morning, swap with another member through the online group rather than leaving the task unfilled.

Noah: And can visitors come to the garden?

Coordinator: Visitors are welcome during open hours, but children must stay with an adult and nobody should pick produce without asking. The garden is a working community space, not an unmanned public park.

Welcome to the new Central Library. The building has three public floors, and each has a different atmosphere. The ground floor is the busiest because it contains the entrance desk, café and children's collection. The first floor is designed for general study. If you need the quietest place, continue to the second floor, where conversations are discouraged and phones must be silent.

Tablets are available from the technology desk. They can be borrowed for one day, not a week, and must be returned before the library closes. Headphones are supplied, but visitors should bring their own charger if possible.

On Friday evenings, the library hosts a conversation group for new residents who want to practise everyday English and meet neighbours. It is informal, so participants are not expected to give a presentation. A separate workshop for teachers runs on Tuesday mornings.

The children's storytelling room used to be beside the café. It was moved because the noise from the café made it difficult for children to hear the storyteller. The new room is on the ground floor near the main windows. Those windows were replaced last year, but that was not the reason for the move.

Most services are available without booking. The exception is the local-history advice desk, because researchers may need an hour with a specialist and several archive boxes. Computer access and printing are managed with a queueing system.

The building also has several practical facilities. The ground-floor lockers are free for four hours, but food cannot be stored in them. The technology desk can lend chargers and adaptors, while the accessibility desk can arrange a height-adjustable table. These services are available during staffed hours, which finish before the building closes on Sundays.

Here is a floor-by-floor guide. The ground floor has children's books and picture books. The first floor has newspapers and magazines, including historical editions on microfilm. The second floor contains the recording studio and the language-learning computers. The roof garden is reached by a staircase from the second floor. It is open when weather and staffing permit.

Supervisor: Your proposal on food waste in student residences has improved, but I want to revisit the method.

Marcus: We first planned to ask residents how much food they had thrown away during the previous month.

Supervisor: That relies on memory. People forget small events and tend to report what they think is acceptable.

Priya: We then considered collecting waste from the restaurant, but we couldn't tell whether it came from students, staff or visitors.

Supervisor: Exactly. Use the communal disposal point in two residence blocks. Weigh the waste there and separate it into agreed categories. Do not work in bedrooms; that would create privacy and access problems.

Elena: We have a set of scales, but Marcus thinks they're not precise enough.

Marcus: They measure to the nearest 100 grams. A small sample of fruit peel could disappear in the rounding.

Supervisor: For a campus study, that precision is acceptable if you record it consistently. Add the measurement limit to your method section.

Elena: We're also unsure how to handle liquids. Soup or milk can add a lot of weight, but it behaves differently from solid food.

Supervisor: Define that before you begin. You might record liquid separately or use a consistent absorbent material, but do not make a decision halfway through the collection. Your categories need to be practical for the volunteers and transparent to a reader.

Priya: We'll photograph the samples before sorting them, then.

Priya: We also want to photograph each sample.

Supervisor: Good. Photographs will not check the scales in a technical sense, but they will record how the categories look and make disagreements easier to review.

Elena: We're worried that our volunteers will be unusually environmentally aware.

Supervisor: That is a real sampling issue. A participant who already separates waste may behave differently. Record their prior habits rather than pretending the problem does not exist.

Marcus: Should we ask about shopping habits? Someone who buys in bulk may have a different pattern from someone who shops daily.

Supervisor: Yes. Shopping frequency and meal planning are useful background variables. You need not build a full economic model, but you should know what other factor might explain the pattern.

Priya: The dining hall changed its portion sizes last week. Could that matter?

Supervisor: Certainly. If residents now take less food there, the residence waste may fall for a reason unrelated to your intervention. Note the date and treat the change as a possible confounding event.

Elena: We have only five volunteers. Should we start immediately?

Supervisor: Run a pilot study for two evenings. It will show whether the categories are clear and whether the scale is practical. Your full data session must finish before the cleaners begin at 6 a.m.

Marcus: How should we explain the results?

Supervisor: Avoid claiming a single cause. Present competing explanations, then say which are better supported by your observations.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.instructions: Play the synthetic recording once. Read the question limits carefully before you begin.
parts.transcript:
Today we'll examine habit formation, beginning with a distinction. A goal is an outcome we want, such as reading more or exercising. A habit is a behaviour repeated in a fairly stable context. The context may include a time, a place, an emotional state or a preceding action. A familiar cue tells the brain that a particular response is available.

The classic habit sequence is cue, routine and reward. The reward need not be dramatic. A feeling of completion, social approval or reduced effort can make the behaviour more likely to be repeated. This explains why a goal alone is often insufficient. People can sincerely want to save money while continuing to respond to the cue of an online sale.

Modern behaviour research questions the idea that success is mainly a contest of willpower. Choices are shaped by their surroundings. If fruit is visible and prepared while sweets are hidden in a cupboard, one choice has lower friction. In behaviour design, friction means a barrier that makes an action less convenient. Adding a small barrier to an unwanted behaviour can be more reliable than demanding constant self-control.

This is not an argument for manipulating people without consent. It is an argument for designing one's own environment. Put a book beside the kettle, prepare sports clothes before bed, or remove a shopping application from the first screen. These adjustments reduce the number of decisions required.

Social surroundings can operate in the same way as physical ones. A colleague who leaves for a walk at lunch creates a cue and a source of accountability, while a group that expects messages late at night can reinforce a different routine. Social support is not simply encouragement; it changes what behaviour feels normal and what action is easy to repeat.

However, a design that works for one person may be intrusive for another. A reminder can become background noise, and a public commitment can create embarrassment when circumstances change. Good behaviour design offers choice and allows a person to revise the plan. The aim is to reduce unnecessary friction, not to make a single routine compulsory.

Reminders can help, but a reminder saying "be healthier" is vague. It works better when paired with a clear action: "After making tea, walk for ten minutes." The existing routine acts as an anchor. Researchers call this habit stacking, although the label matters less than the precise link between the old and new behaviours.

Measurement is useful because intentions and actions diverge. A person may believe they study every evening, but a simple record can show three sessions a week. The record is not a moral judgement; it is evidence about context. It may reveal that the behaviour disappears on days when the person travels or sleeps poorly.

Missing one day is not usually a biological disaster. The danger is the interpretation that follows. Some people treat an interruption as proof that they have failed and abandon the attempt altogether. A more useful rule is to resume at the next opportunity. Consistency matters, but perfection is not a realistic definition of a stable habit.

In conclusion, lasting change is not one heroic decision produced by motivation. It is a process in which cues make an action visible, the action is practical enough to perform, and feedback helps the person adjust. Personality affects the process, but context is often the part we can change most easily.

parts.title: Passage 1
parts.passage:
[1] Modern agriculture depends on a surprisingly narrow range of plants. Thousands of edible species exist, but global food production is concentrated in a small number of crops, and within those crops many farms use genetically similar varieties. Uniformity can improve harvesting and marketing, yet it creates vulnerability. A disease that affects one widely planted variety may threaten fields across a large region. Seed banks are one response to this risk: they collect, dry and store seeds so that genetic material remains available for future breeding.

[2] The most famous collections are not intended to replace living agriculture. A seed bank is an insurance policy, not a museum in which plants are permanently removed from the world. Seeds may be withdrawn when breeders need traits such as drought tolerance, resistance to a fungus or a shorter growing season. The difficult work begins after retrieval. A useful trait may be hidden among many genes, and transferring it into a commercially suitable variety can take years.

[3] Storage conditions must be carefully controlled. Many seeds tolerate drying and freezing, but not all. Orthodox seeds can often be dried to a low moisture content and stored at sub-zero temperatures. Recalcitrant seeds, including some tropical species, are damaged by drying and are much harder to preserve. For these plants, collections may maintain living trees, tissue cultures or carefully managed field plots. A single storage method cannot protect every crop.

[4] Records are as important as refrigerators. A sample without a reliable name, collection location and date may be difficult to use. Curators also record the conditions in which a plant grew, although such information is not always complete. Duplicate samples in different institutions reduce the chance that a fire, power failure or political crisis will destroy a unique collection.

[5] There is a difference between conserving diversity and making it available. Some collections hold seeds safely but lack the staff or funding to test germination regularly. Seeds are living material; their viability declines. Periodic regeneration requires growing plants, allowing them to flower and collecting fresh seed. If regeneration is done carelessly, unwanted cross-pollination can change the genetic identity of the sample.

[6] Farmers remain essential to conservation. A variety grown in a field continues to adapt to local pests, soil and climate. When a seed is stored in a freezer, that ongoing relationship stops. Community seed networks and farmer-led breeding therefore complement large institutions. They may also preserve knowledge about taste, cooking quality and cultural use-qualities that are poorly captured by a laboratory description.

[7] Climate change makes the task more urgent but not simpler. A variety selected for one historical climate may not perform in a future one. Breeders need access to broad collections, yet they must avoid assuming that a single gene will solve a complex problem. Drought response, for example, may involve roots, flowering time, soil microbes and farming practice. The value of a seed bank lies partly in keeping options open while researchers learn which combinations matter.

[8] Access to those options is a matter of governance as well as biology. Seeds collected in one country may be stored in another, and researchers need agreements about exchange, acknowledgement and benefit sharing. Farmers who have maintained a variety for generations may reasonably ask whether commercial use should return value to their communities. A collection can be technically open while remaining practically inaccessible if requests are slow, fees are high or the catalogue is difficult to search.

[9] Breeding programmes also face a choice between broad testing and rapid release. A new variety may perform well in a controlled plot but fail when grown by farmers with fewer inputs. Testing across soils, seasons and management systems takes time, yet it exposes weaknesses that laboratory performance hides. Seed banks support this work by making diversity available; they do not decide which trait is most valuable without collaboration with the people who will grow and eat the crop.

[10] The distinction between preservation and use is therefore important. A packet in a vault represents possibility, not food security by itself. Security emerges when storage, records, breeding, farmer knowledge and fair distribution operate together.

[11] The public image of a seed bank is often a locked vault. In practice, it is a network of people, records, laboratories, farms and international agreements. Its success is measured not by the number of packets stored but by whether diverse, well-documented material can be used responsibly when conditions change.

[12] Storage facilities must prepare for ordinary failures as well as dramatic disasters. Freezers need power, backup generators and alarms, while staff need procedures for checking moisture and germination. A collection can lose value gradually when a small decline in viability goes unnoticed. Regular audits are therefore less visible than the vault itself but just as important. They turn preservation from a one-time act into a continuing responsibility.

[13] The work is especially difficult for crops that reproduce through cuttings or require living tissue. A field collection may preserve a tree's diversity more faithfully than a freezer, but it is exposed to storms, pests and political change. Institutions sometimes maintain several forms of the same material so that a failure in one method does not destroy the whole sample. Redundancy costs money, yet it is the principle that makes insurance useful.

[14] Public funding often favours dramatic new facilities, while the less visible work of cleaning records and testing germination competes with them. A balanced programme reserves money for staff and training. Without that investment, a vault may contain impressive diversity that no breeder can confidently identify or request.

parts.title: Passage 2
parts.passage:
[1] As cities warm, shade has become a subject for architects, public-health researchers and transport planners. A shaded street may feel several degrees cooler than an exposed one, but the experience depends on more than air temperature. People exchange heat with surrounding walls and pavement, lose heat through evaporation and adjust their behaviour according to wind, humidity and activity. Shade is therefore both a physical condition and a social resource: a route that is technically cooler is not useful if it is unpleasant, inaccessible or unsafe.

[2] The simplest source of shade is a building. Narrow streets can block the sun for much of the day, and arcades create sheltered edges between indoor and outdoor space. Yet dense construction can also restrict air movement and store heat in masonry after sunset. A design that provides excellent midday shade may make a neighbourhood uncomfortable at night. Architects increasingly model shade across several hours rather than judging a façade from a single photograph.

[3] Trees provide a different kind of protection. Their leaves block radiation, while transpiration can cool the surrounding air. Mature trees also offer psychological benefits: people may choose to walk along a tree-lined street even when the measured temperature is similar to that of a paved route. The disadvantage is time. A newly planted tree offers little shade for years, and a species selected without regard to soil, water and root space may fail before it matures.

[4] Temporary structures can respond more quickly. Fabric canopies, retractable awnings and modular shade frames are useful for markets, school yards and emergency cooling sites. They are easier to relocate than trees or buildings, but they require maintenance and may be damaged by wind. Their visual presence can also raise questions about who controls public space. A canopy installed for a festival may be welcomed; the same structure outside a shop may be seen as an obstruction.

[5] Shade policy can unintentionally favour some users. A path under trees may be comfortable for a walker but difficult for someone using a wheelchair if roots lift the pavement. A dark, enclosed arcade may provide relief from heat but cause people to feel unsafe. Parents, older adults, street vendors and delivery workers may need places to stop rather than a continuous route. Effective design therefore begins with observation of how people actually move and rest.

[6] The economic benefits of shade are often described in terms of reduced energy use. If buildings remain cooler, demand for air conditioning may fall. That result is possible, but it is not automatic. External shading must be combined with ventilation, insulation and appropriate window design. Otherwise occupants may simply use cooling equipment more intensively. On a city scale, shade can also protect road surfaces and reduce heat-related illness, although these benefits are hard to assign to one project.

[7] Researchers use a mixture of tools to evaluate shade. Satellite images show tree canopy, while sensors measure temperature, radiation and humidity at pedestrian height. Interviews reveal whether people perceive a route as comfortable. These data can disagree. A shaded path may record a modest temperature reduction but attract more users because it feels calmer. Conversely, a visually green space may be avoided because benches are poorly located or the surface becomes muddy.

[8] The material beneath a shade structure matters too. Dark asphalt absorbs solar energy and may continue radiating heat after the sun has moved away, whereas a permeable or lighter surface can change the balance. Reflective materials are not harmless by default: they may redirect glare towards windows or pedestrians. Design teams must consider the experience at eye level, not only the temperature recorded by an instrument.

[9] Maintenance is often the hidden limit. Canopies need cleaning and inspection, trees need pruning and watering, and drainage around a planted area must remain open. If responsibility is divided between a transport agency, a parks department and a private property owner, a small failure can make the route uncomfortable for an entire season. Agreements about maintenance should be made before construction, when budgets and responsibilities are still visible.

[10] Heat planning also benefits from seasonal observation. A place that is pleasant in June may be exposed in September when the sun follows a different path. Schools and markets have their own schedules, so a design based on the busiest hour of the day may miss the period when vulnerable people actually wait outside. Layered shade is valuable partly because it can respond to these changing patterns.

[11] The future of shade design is likely to be layered. Cities will combine permanent trees and buildings with adjustable structures, reflective materials and schedules that respond to seasonal sunlight. The aim is not to cover every surface. It is to offer a connected network of comfortable options while leaving enough open space for ventilation, biodiversity and social activity. Shade is most successful when treated as part of urban infrastructure rather than as decoration added after the important decisions have been made.

[12] Residents should be able to understand why a particular solution was chosen. A canopy may look unnecessary in a photograph taken in winter, while a tree may seem to occupy valuable space before its canopy develops. Public explanations about heat exposure, access and maintenance can make a long-term project easier to support. They also create a way to report unintended effects, such as glare, blocked visibility or a route that becomes inaccessible after rain.

parts.title: Passage 3
parts.passage:
[1] Automated ranking systems are used to sort job applications, recommend university courses, identify suspicious financial transactions and decide which online posts appear first. Their appeal is obvious: a computer can process more information than a human decision-maker and can apply a rule consistently. Yet consistency is not the same as fairness. If the data reflect unequal opportunities, an algorithm may reproduce those inequalities with an appearance of objectivity.

[2] The first difficulty is defining the target. Suppose an employer asks a system to identify applicants likely to succeed. Does "succeed" mean staying in the job, receiving a high performance rating or earning a promotion? Each measure captures something different. A system trained on promotion records may learn the preferences of earlier managers rather than the abilities of applicants. A system trained on retention may favour people whose personal circumstances resemble those of current employees.

[3] Data can enter a system in several ways. Historical labels may encode past decisions; features may act as indirect proxies for protected characteristics; and missing data may be unevenly distributed. A postcode, for example, can correlate with income, language background or access to transport without explicitly naming any of them. Removing a sensitive variable does not necessarily remove its influence if other variables carry similar information.

[4] Fairness researchers have proposed statistical tests, but these tests can conflict. One measure may require equal error rates across groups, while another requires equal positive prediction rates. When groups differ in the prevalence of an outcome, satisfying both conditions may be mathematically impossible without changing the decision rule. This does not make fairness meaningless; it means that a technical metric cannot settle a question that also involves values and consequences.

[5] Transparency is often offered as the remedy. If developers explain which variables matter, affected people may challenge errors. But transparency has several meanings. A model can be open-source and still be incomprehensible to a non-specialist. Conversely, a simple explanation may conceal uncertainty. Meaningful transparency should include information about purpose, data quality, performance across groups and the route for appeal.

[6] Human oversight is not a guaranteed safeguard. A reviewer may simply accept the computer's recommendation, especially when the system is described as highly accurate. This is sometimes called automation bias. Oversight is more credible when reviewers have time, authority and information to disagree, and when the organisation records what happened after an appeal. A human signature at the end of a process is not enough if the human cannot alter the outcome.

[7] Some designers favour participatory development. People affected by a ranking system can identify harms that are invisible in a dataset, such as the difficulty of correcting a record or the cost of being repeatedly misclassified. Participation does not remove conflicts of interest and cannot represent every possible user, but it can widen the definition of the problem before a system is deployed.

[8] Procurement decisions can determine whether those concerns are heard. An institution may buy a finished system from a vendor and discover that its data cannot be exported or its performance cannot be independently checked. A requirement for documentation, testing and an appeal process should be written into the contract before implementation. Otherwise, responsibility becomes unclear: the vendor can point to the client's instructions, while the client can point to the vendor's technical expertise.

[9] Fairness also concerns time. A person wrongly rejected from one opportunity may lose access to later opportunities because the decision becomes part of a record. A rapid automated process can therefore create a slow accumulation of disadvantage. Reviewers should ask how long an outcome lasts, who can amend it and whether an error is likely to be repeated by another system. These questions are often more concrete for affected people than an abstract debate about model architecture.

[10] Documentation should describe uncertainty rather than hide it. A model card or impact report can state the population on which a system was tested, the situations in which it should not be used and the groups for whom errors were higher. Such documents do not solve the problem, but they make future monitoring and challenge possible. In a changing institution, a forgotten assumption can be as damaging as a coding error.

[11] Regulation is moving unevenly. Some institutions require impact assessments, documentation and monitoring; others rely on voluntary principles. Monitoring matters because a model may perform acceptably at launch and deteriorate as behaviour, populations or incentives change. An algorithm is not a neutral machine installed once. It is part of a social process in which people adapt to the categories it creates.

[12] The central lesson is not that automated ranking must be abandoned. It is that efficiency claims should be evaluated alongside error, distribution and recourse. A system that saves staff time but makes correction impossible may transfer costs to applicants. A system that predicts accurately for one group and poorly for another may be useful only after its purpose is narrowed. Fair ranking requires technical skill, institutional responsibility and a willingness to treat affected people as participants rather than data points.

[13] This responsibility extends to retirement. Institutions should decide when a system has failed, become obsolete or no longer serves the purpose for which it was approved. Keeping a model in operation simply because replacing it is inconvenient can make an early compromise permanent. A clear review date, a record of complaints and a budget for correction make it easier to stop or redesign a system before harm becomes routine.

parts.transcript:
Guide: Harbour Cycle Tours, how may I help?

Aisha: I'd like to book a tour for my parents and me. The family name is Morrison.

Guide: We have places on 18 July and 20 July.

Aisha: The 18th is better. Where do we meet?

Guide: Outside the market station, by the clock. The group leaves at 9:30. Please arrive fifteen minutes earlier for fitting.

Aisha: How long is the standard route?

Guide: Three hours, including two short stops. We also run a five-hour coastal route, but most families choose the standard one.

Aisha: What does the fee include?

Guide: A bicycle and a helmet. We have a few electric bikes, but those cost extra and need to be requested in advance.

Aisha: We'll bring water. Is that necessary?

Guide: Yes, please bring a bottle of water. There's a refill point halfway, but carrying some is sensible.

Aisha: What will we see?

Guide: The route follows the river and stops at a former shipyard. It used to build fishing boats; now it's an arts centre.

Aisha: My father has a back problem. Could he have a padded seat?

Guide: Certainly. I'll mark that request. We also have a lower frame if mounting is difficult.

Aisha: Are there places to stop if one of us gets tired?

Guide: Yes. The first stop is beside the old customs house, after about forty minutes. The second is at the shipyard café, although buying food there is optional. The guide rides at the back of the group, and nobody is expected to race. If a participant feels unwell, we can shorten the route and return along the riverside path.

Aisha: Do we need special clothes?

Guide: Comfortable shoes and a light waterproof layer are sensible. Helmets are compulsory, and reflective bands are supplied for the return section if the group is delayed.

Aisha: And if the weather is terrible?

Guide: You can cancel without charge up to 24 hours before departure. After that, the fee is normally retained, unless we cancel for safety.

parts.transcript:
Welcome to the Harbour Lights Festival. Although there will be visiting performers from three countries, the festival's main purpose this year is to celebrate local maritime history. Many activities use stories collected from retired fishermen and dock workers.

Visitors arriving by train should enter through Gate 2, which is closest to the information tent. Gate 1 is for residents with bicycles, while Gate 3 opens later for evening ticket holders.

The lantern workshop is open to children aged eight and above. Younger children may watch with an adult, but the wire frames and small tools are not suitable for them. Once made, lanterns can be carried to the riverbank and placed along the marked path. Please do not take them home, because they form part of the evening display.

The parade normally crosses the old stone bridge. This year the bridge is being repaired, so the route is shorter and ends before the ferry terminal. It has not been shortened because the route is steep, and performers are arriving on time.

The festival also has a quiet zone for visitors who prefer less crowded spaces. It is located behind the maritime archive and has benches, drinking water and a volunteer information desk. Food stalls accept cards, but the craft workshop accepts only small cash payments because it is run by local artists. Lost children should be taken to the information tent rather than to an individual performance area.

Here is today's programme. The boat-building demonstration begins at 10:00 beside the dry dock. The children's lantern workshop starts at 11:30 in the sail loft. At 13:00, a harbour clean-up leaves from the west gate; gloves and bags are supplied. The oral-history talk is at 14:15 in the warehouse theatre. Finally, the evening parade starts at 19:30, after the lanterns have been collected from the workshop.

parts.transcript:
Supervisor 1: Your review contains plenty of reading, but at present it is mostly a sequence of summaries.

Daniel: So it's too descriptive?

Supervisor 1: Exactly. A literature review should show how studies relate. You might group them by research question and method, rather than simply moving from the oldest article to the newest.

Supervisor 2: Also be cautious about treating publication date as progress. An older study may use a smaller sample but ask a question that newer papers ignore.

Daniel: I found one early paper whose result is often cited. The participants were all volunteers from the same software company.

Supervisor 1: Check whether later authors have cited it for a population it never studied. A limitation can disappear from the secondary literature when a short summary is repeated often enough.

Daniel: I've also found several papers that use the word "productivity" without defining it.

Supervisor 2: Then record that in your comparison table. A measure can be objective without being equivalent across studies. If one paper counts completed tasks and another asks participants how productive they felt, their results should not be placed on one scale without explanation.

Supervisor 2: Then say so. The study may be informative, but its sample limits generalization. Were the participants selected because they already had a particular interest?

Daniel: We don't know. The paper is vague about recruitment.

Supervisor 1: That is another limitation, not a reason to delete it.

Daniel: Two studies report opposite results about whether background music affects concentration.

Supervisor 2: Before calling that a contradiction, check how "concentration" was defined. One may measure task accuracy and the other may measure time-on-task. Different operational definitions can produce apparently conflicting findings.

Supervisor 1: And don't exclude a result just because it is inconvenient. Explain the difference and say what evidence would resolve it.

Daniel: Which sources should I add? I have mostly studies from Britain.

Supervisor 2: Add a recent systematic review so you can position your selection within the wider evidence.

Supervisor 1: And a study from a different country. The context may affect how people use background sound, so geographical variety will strengthen the discussion.

Daniel: I'll add those. Should I include a newspaper editorial about productivity?

Supervisor 2: Only if you analyse it as public commentary, not as research evidence. It is not essential to your review.

Daniel: I'm struggling to keep track of the methods.

Supervisor 1: Make a comparison table with columns for sample, measure, result and limitation. It will help you see patterns, but do not paste the table into the final text without interpretation.

Daniel: When should I send the new version?

Supervisor 2: By the 28th. That gives us two days before the departmental meeting.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.instructions: Play the synthetic recording once. Read the question limits carefully before you begin.
parts.transcript:
Today's lecture is about underwater soundscapes. Sound behaves differently in water: it travels faster because water is more dense than air, and it can travel long distances with relatively little loss. Marine animals have exploited this physical environment for millions of years. Whales use calls to find partners and maintain social contact, while dolphins use clicks for echolocation.

The modern ocean contains a new acoustic layer produced by engines, propellers, construction and sonar. Shipping noise is concentrated along coastal routes, which are also areas where many animals feed or migrate. The issue is not that every ship is equally loud at every moment. Noise varies with vessel design, speed, sea conditions and distance from the listener.

Researchers describe one effect as masking. A human-made sound makes an animal's signal harder to detect, much as a conversation becomes difficult beside a loud road. Masking can reduce the distance over which a whale hears a call or can force an animal to spend more energy repeating it. A dolphin has been observed shifting the frequency of its call in a noisy environment, although such changes may not always solve the problem.

Noise may also affect behaviour without directly blocking a call. An animal can avoid a feeding site, surface at a different time or move away from a preferred nursery area. These responses are difficult to interpret because the same movement may be caused by food availability, temperature or predators. Researchers therefore prefer repeated observations that combine sound recordings with information about habitat and season.

Construction noise has a different pattern from shipping. Pile driving can be extremely intense but temporary, while engines create a lower-level background that persists along a route. Regulations may need different thresholds for these sources. A short, predictable closure of a construction area may protect animals more effectively than a general rule that ignores when the loudest activity occurs.

Studying the effect is challenging because shipping noise overlaps with waves, rain and the calls of other animals. It also varies geographically. A hydrophone-a microphone designed for water-can record these sounds. Researchers use multiple hydrophones to build an acoustic map, then compare periods of high and low traffic. They may combine recordings with observations of animal movement and behaviour.

Possible responses range from changing shipping lanes to reducing vessel speed during breeding or migration periods. Slower ships generally produce less engine and propeller noise and give large animals more time to avoid collision. The measure may have economic costs, so timing and location matter. A temporary speed reduction in a narrow corridor may be more practical than a permanent rule across an entire sea.

The policy question is therefore not "Can we make the ocean silent?" It is whether activity can be arranged so that important biological signals remain usable. Effective decisions combine acoustic evidence with knowledge of species, routes, seasons and maritime operations. Listening to the ocean is a scientific task, but acting on what is heard also requires practical planning.

modules.title: Reading

parts.title: Passage 1
parts.passage:
[1] Human sleep is timed by an interaction between internal biology and external signals. The most influential signal is light, especially the change from daylight to darkness. Cells in the eye communicate information about environmental brightness to a region of the brain that helps coordinate circadian rhythms. This system does not force everyone to sleep at one identical hour, but it helps align alertness and rest with the twenty-four-hour cycle.

[2] Electric lighting extended the useful day. It made evening education, industrial work and social activity possible, and it reduced dependence on seasonal daylight. The same flexibility can weaken the difference between day and night. Bright light late in the evening can delay the internal timing of sleep, particularly when it contains a strong short-wavelength component. Screens are often blamed, but the total brightness, distance from the eyes and duration of exposure also matter.

[3] Sleep loss is not caused by light alone. Work schedules, stress, noise, caring responsibilities and illness can all disturb rest. Yet light is attractive to researchers and designers because it can be measured and changed. A bedroom lamp can be dimmed, a phone can use a warmer display and a building can adjust its lighting schedule. These interventions may help, although they cannot compensate for every social cause of poor sleep.

[4] Morning light has a different role from evening light. Exposure soon after waking can help move the body clock earlier, while late light may move it later. This is why shift workers and travellers use carefully timed light rather than simply seeking as much brightness as possible. The same lamp can have different effects depending on when it is used.

[5] Individual timing matters. Some people naturally feel alert early, while others reach their best concentration later in the day. These chronotypes are not entirely fixed, but they influence how strongly a person experiences an evening schedule. A recommendation that works for an early riser may be difficult for someone whose employment begins late. Researchers therefore examine both the average effect of light and the variation between people.

[6] The strength of a light intervention also depends on the background. Outdoor daylight is usually far brighter than indoor lighting, even when a room feels comfortable. A short walk outside may expose the eyes to more useful morning light than sitting beside a bright screen. At night, a small source close to the face can be more significant than a larger lamp across a room. Distance and direction are practical design variables.

[7] These details help explain why studies sometimes seem to disagree. One experiment may use a bright, carefully timed stimulus under controlled conditions, while another observes ordinary household behaviour. Both can be informative, but their findings should not be combined as if they measured exactly the same exposure.

[8] School and workplace design increasingly considers these differences. A classroom with good daylight may support alertness, but glare can make reading difficult. Offices that expose workers to outdoor light may improve satisfaction without guaranteeing better sleep. Researchers therefore distinguish between subjective reports, such as feeling more energetic, and objective measures, such as sleep timing or duration.

[9] There is also a cultural dimension. Some communities have evening routines that include bright shops, television or outdoor gatherings, while others maintain darker domestic spaces. Advice that treats one schedule as universally healthy may ignore work, climate and family life. A realistic intervention should preserve useful evening activity while reducing unnecessary exposure close to bedtime.

[10] The strongest evidence does not support a simple message that all screens are harmful. It suggests that regular timing, sufficient darkness for sleep and appropriate morning light are helpful conditions. People differ, and a small change may matter more than an expensive device. Turning down unnecessary lights, keeping a phone away from the bed and seeking daylight early in the day are modest measures, but they address the underlying relationship between environment and body clock.

[11] Public advice should also distinguish between occasional disruption and a persistent pattern. A late film or an overnight journey may shift sleep temporarily without creating a long-term problem. Repeated exposure, especially when combined with irregular work, can make the body clock harder to predict. Schools and employers can help by giving people some control over schedules, providing access to daylight and avoiding the assumption that a single bedtime rule suits every timetable.

[12] Designers should be cautious about using sleep technology as a substitute for ordinary conditions. A lamp that claims to imitate sunrise may be useful for someone in a dark winter room, but its effect depends on timing and intensity. A wearable device may estimate sleep, yet the estimate is not identical to a clinical measurement. Such tools can support experimentation, but users should not interpret a number as a diagnosis without appropriate advice.

[13] The same caution applies to children and adolescents, whose schedules are shaped by school and family rules. Delaying school start times may help some students, but transport, childcare and after-school work can limit what a community can change. The useful question is how lighting, schedules and social obligations interact, not whether one device or rule can solve sleep loss alone.
