parts.title: Passage 2
parts.passage:
[1] Citizen science is often introduced as a way to collect more observations than professional researchers could gather alone. Volunteers count butterflies, photograph plants, record rainfall or report the timing of bird migration. Their contributions can cover large areas and long periods. The value of the data, however, depends on how observations are made, what participants choose to record and whether researchers can account for uneven effort.

[2] The unevenness is not a defect that disappears when a project becomes popular. A woodland beside a city may receive hundreds of observations while a remote valley receives none. People tend to visit attractive or accessible places, and experienced volunteers may record unusual species more readily than common ones. A map of observations may therefore represent human movement as much as animal distribution.

[3] Project design can reduce some of these biases. Organizers may ask participants to follow a fixed route, spend a specified length of time searching or report every species rather than only unusual sightings. Training photographs and short tests improve identification. The aim is not to turn every volunteer into a professional taxonomist; it is to create a shared protocol that makes observations comparable.

[4] Technology has expanded participation. A phone can attach location and time to a photograph, and an application can suggest possible species. Automated suggestions are useful but not infallible. A confident-looking image match may be wrong when two species have similar leaves or calls. Projects that accept automatic identifications without review risk creating a large database whose apparent precision exceeds its real accuracy.

[5] Volunteers are not merely unpaid instruments. They may notice changes that a narrow research question overlooks, and they often possess local knowledge about weather, land management or unusual events. In successful projects, researchers explain how the information will be used and report findings back to participants. Feedback sustains attention and turns data collection into a form of public learning.

[6] Ethics also matter. Photographing a rare nest can reveal its location to curious visitors. Recording on private land requires permission, and communities may object if data are used to restrict their livelihood without consultation. A project that asks for public participation must clarify ownership, privacy and the consequences of publication.

[7] The strongest citizen-science datasets combine volunteer observations with other sources. Satellite images can provide continuous coverage, while professional surveys offer carefully standardized samples. The sources do not need to agree perfectly. Differences may reveal where each method is sensitive or where environmental change is occurring. What matters is that researchers understand the limits of each dataset rather than treating a large number of records as automatic proof.

[8] Volunteer retention is another methodological issue. A project may begin with enthusiastic participants and gradually lose people when the task becomes repetitive or when feedback is absent. If only the most committed volunteers remain, later observations may look more reliable while actually representing a narrower group. Reminders, training updates and public summaries can support participation, but organizers should still record how effort changed over time.

[9] Validation can be targeted rather than universal. Professional observers might revisit a small sample of locations or check records that a computer identifies as unusual. This does not mean that volunteer data are assumed to be wrong; it means that the project has a way to estimate error. The validation strategy should be announced in advance so that a surprising result is not quietly discarded after it appears.

[10] Equity affects who gets to contribute. A project requiring a recent smartphone may exclude older residents or communities with limited connectivity, while a paper route or local meeting may include people who are rarely represented online. Providing several ways to participate can improve both fairness and data coverage. It also signals that expertise is not limited to people who already use scientific vocabulary.

[11] Citizen science is therefore best understood as a partnership. Its scale can transform research questions, but scale is not the same as quality. With clear protocols, appropriate verification and honest communication, volunteers can help monitor changing ecosystems and ask questions that would otherwise remain invisible. Without those safeguards, the project may produce impressive maps and weak conclusions.

[12] Publication should make the uncertainty visible. A map can show where observations were submitted, but it should also show search effort, gaps and confidence. A public audience may prefer a clean image with no blank areas, while a researcher needs to know whether a blank means absence or simply no visit. Explaining that distinction is not a weakness. It helps volunteers see why careful recording matters and prevents policy-makers from treating a convenient image as a complete survey.

[13] The relationship can last beyond one project. Volunteers who learn to identify a plant may later notice a new disease, participate in a different survey or ask local authorities about habitat management. Researchers gain continuity, while participants gain a more detailed understanding of their surroundings. This outcome is difficult to measure in a spreadsheet, but it can be part of the project's public value when it is reported honestly rather than used to exaggerate scientific certainty.

[14] Projects should also plan for disagreement about findings. A volunteer may believe a species was present when a reviewer does not accept the photograph, or residents may challenge a conclusion that appears to criticize local land use. Publishing the protocol and the route for correction allows the evidence to be debated without turning one disputed record into a personal conflict.

parts.title: Passage 3
parts.passage:
[1] Algorithmic systems increasingly determine what people see, which applications receive attention and how scarce opportunities are distributed. Their advocates emphasize speed and consistency. Critics reply that a system can be consistently wrong, or consistently disadvantage a group, while appearing neutral because its instructions are mathematical. The debate is often presented as a choice between human judgement and machine calculation. That framing is misleading: algorithms are designed by people, trained on social records and used within institutions.

[2] Fairness begins before a model is selected. An organisation must decide what outcome it is trying to produce and whose interests count. A hospital predicting readmission may want to allocate support, while an insurer may want to price risk. The same prediction can serve different purposes, and a model appropriate for one purpose may be harmful in another. Asking whether an algorithm is fair without naming its use leaves the central question undefined.

[3] Data quality is not only a matter of missing values. A dataset may be accurate about the past and still unsuitable for the future. If earlier decisions were shaped by unequal access to education, transport or credit, a model may treat those inequalities as evidence of merit or risk. Historical data also record what institutions chose to notice. A person who never applied for a position does not appear as an unsuccessful applicant, even if barriers prevented the application.

[4] Developers often search for a variable that predicts outcomes well. Prediction can be valuable, but accuracy is not a complete ethical standard. A system may be accurate overall while making more serious errors for a small group. It may also predict a person's behaviour without offering a fair opportunity to change the circumstances behind that prediction. In high-stakes settings, the cost of a false positive and a false negative should be made explicit.

[5] There is no single mathematical definition of fairness. Equal treatment may mean equal error rates, equal access to opportunity or equal benefit from an intervention. These goals can conflict when groups have different histories and outcome rates. Technical metrics can reveal trade-offs, but they cannot decide which trade-off society should accept. That decision belongs to a legitimate governance process, not to the software by default.

[6] Governance should continue after deployment. A model can drift as people change behaviour in response to it, as economic conditions shift or as the data pipeline is altered. Monitoring should therefore examine outcomes across groups, investigate complaints and record decisions to update or withdraw the system. Independent audits can help, but an audit is useful only when someone has the authority to act on its findings.

[7] People affected by automated decisions need recourse. They should know that a system was involved, understand the broad reason for an outcome and have a realistic way to challenge an error. Complete access to source code may not be necessary for every person, but secrecy should not prevent correction. An explanation that uses technical jargon without identifying a possible remedy is transparency in name rather than in practice.

[8] Recourse must be timely. An appeal that takes six months is of little use when a person needs a job, a loan or access to a service this week. Institutions should set deadlines, preserve relevant records and ensure that an appeal is reviewed by someone who was not responsible for the original automated recommendation. In some cases the appropriate remedy is not to adjust one record but to reconsider whether the system should be used for that purpose at all.

[9] Privacy adds another layer of responsibility. Data collected for one decision may be reused to train a different system, creating a purpose that the original participants did not expect. De-identification reduces some risks but cannot guarantee anonymity when several datasets are combined. Clear retention rules and limits on secondary use are therefore part of fair design, not administrative detail.

[10] Public institutions may also need to explain why automation was chosen. If a human review would be slower but more appropriate for a high-stakes case, efficiency alone is not a sufficient reason to automate. A narrow system used with consent and correction may be more defensible than a broad system that quietly ranks everyone.

[11] The case for fair algorithms is therefore a case for disciplined institutions. Good design matters, but so do purpose, data history, human responsibility and the ability to repair harm. Automation can support decisions, especially when it makes patterns visible or distributes resources consistently. It should not be allowed to hide a value choice behind a numerical score. Fairness is not a property that a model possesses forever; it is a relationship that must be maintained.

[12] This relationship should include a clear end point. Institutions need criteria for suspending a model, replacing it or returning a decision to human review. A system can become unsuitable when the population changes, when a new law alters the purpose or when repeated appeals reveal a pattern of harm. Keeping it in operation because it is familiar transfers the cost of uncertainty to the people being ranked. Review dates, complaint records and public reporting make correction possible before an early compromise becomes permanent.

[13] The same principle applies to models used in low-stakes settings. A recommendation that is merely inconvenient may still shape what a person learns, buys or believes over time. Small rankings accumulate, and an apparently harmless preference can narrow the range of opportunities presented to someone. Periodic testing against varied users helps reveal these effects before the system is trusted in a more consequential setting.

Administrator: Good evening, City Learning Centre. Are you registering for a course?

Farid: Yes. My surname is Kovacs, and I'm interested in business English.

Administrator: We have general, academic and business English. The business course begins on 16 September and runs for ten weeks.

Farid: Tuesdays and Thursdays, I think?

Administrator: Correct, from 6:30 to 8:00. Classes are in Room 14, on the first floor.

Farid: Is there a textbook?

Administrator: You'll need to buy the course workbook. The teacher provides extra articles online.

Farid: When is the first assessment?

Administrator: In the second week. It's a short presentation, not a written exam.

Farid: I'll be driving. Is parking possible?

Administrator: The centre's car park is reserved before eight, but students may use it after 6:00 p.m. Actually, because your class starts at half past six, that's fine.

If the result is unclear, the teacher will speak to you during the first lesson. Please bring identification and arrive ten minutes early because the reception desk becomes busy at half past six.

parts.transcript:
Welcome to Pine Ridge Reserve. The new visitor route is not a cycle path. It was created mainly to protect a nesting area used by ground-nesting birds, so bicycles must remain on the old road. The route links the car park with the eastern viewing platform and is open from sunrise to sunset.

Although the reserve is cooler than the town, we recommend beginning before midday because the exposed section becomes hotter in the afternoon. The car park rarely fills before lunch, and the ranger station remains open until five.

The boardwalk crosses a wet patch. Its surface is made from recycled plastic produced locally, rather than untreated wood. It can withstand water and does not need regular painting. At the pond, the best view is from the eastern platform. The wooden bridge is useful for crossing the stream, but tall reeds block the view from it.

Dogs must be kept on the marked path and are prohibited within the pond enclosure because they disturb water birds. The ground is stable, and the boardwalk is strong enough for service vehicles.

The complete route is 4.6 kilometres. In dry weather, visitors should carry water, because the only drinking tap is beside the car park. The information hut contains a display about local geology, including the granite formation beneath the ridge.

After the small stream crossing, the path rises sharply. The steepest section begins after the bridge and continues to the shelter. Mobile emergency calls may fail in the hollow near the quarry, so walk back towards the ridge if you need a signal.

The shelter has a rain gauge and a noticeboard showing recent sightings. Please do not feed birds or leave fruit near the platform, since this changes their behaviour and attracts rats. Bin collection is limited, so visitors should take large picnic containers home. Rangers inspect the route each morning, but conditions can change after a storm.

Lecturer: Let's review your project on sustainable packaging. Your first comparison used a glass jar and a plastic pouch, but the products had very different weights and quantities. That makes the comparison unfair.

Omar: We'll compare packaging used for the same amount of sauce.

Nia: We also found that one package was designed to be reused, while the others were intended to be discarded.

Lecturer: That is important. Compare like with like where possible, but keep the use phase visible. A reusable container may have a larger manufacturing footprint and still perform better if it is used many times. Ask your audience to consider the number of uses rather than treating "reusable" as a complete conclusion.

Lecturer: Better. Also define sustainability across the complete life cycle: raw materials, production, transport, use and disposal.

Nia: Our survey asks, "Do you prefer eco-friendly packaging?"

Lecturer: The word sounds clear but is not. Respondents may define it as recyclable, low-carbon, reusable or simply natural. Ask which features they mean, or give a short definition before the question.

Omar: I'm checking the carbon figures, but some assumptions are hidden in the manufacturer's report.

Lecturer: Then flag those assumptions. Don't copy a precise number without explaining its boundary. You are responsible for checking them, but I can help you find the source data.

Nia: I think a cost comparison would make the presentation more practical.

Lecturer: Include it if you can distinguish the price to a customer from the environmental cost. I would also like a comparison graphic, so viewers can see how the three materials differ.

Omar: Glass, aluminium and plastic?

Lecturer: Use paper instead of plastic. Plastic is too broad for the time available; a paper carton will give you a clearer case.

Nia: I'll redesign the survey, then.

Lecturer: Good. Omar, check the assumptions; Nia, revise the survey; and create the comparison graphic together, but let Omar take the first draft because he has the data table.

Nia: Should the graphic show the uncertainty in the carbon estimates?

Lecturer: Yes. Use a note or a range if the source provides one. A single exact-looking number can hide assumptions about transport distance and recycling rates. Your audience does not need a statistics lecture, but it should see where the comparison is firm and where it is provisional.

Omar: How long should we speak?

Lecturer: Twelve minutes maximum. Leave two minutes for questions. Your conclusion must acknowledge a trade-off. A material may perform well in one stage and poorly in another, so do not claim that one is always best.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.instructions: Play the synthetic recording once. Read the question limits carefully before you begin.
parts.transcript:
Urban bees are often discussed as if the city were simply a poor version of the countryside. The reality is more varied. Parks, balconies, vacant lots and gardens can contain a surprising range of flowering plants. Some cities provide flowers from early spring to late autumn, so bees may find food across different seasons.

The timing of flowers matters because a colony may require food before the most visible summer bloom. Early willow or fruit trees can support insects when few garden plants are open, while late ivy can provide resources before winter. A planting plan that looks colourful for one month may create a long gap at another point in the year. Researchers therefore record flowering calendars, not just the number of species.

Urban heat can be an advantage for some insects because plants flower earlier, but heat and drought can also shorten the period in which nectar is available. Watering a garden may help plants, yet shallow containers can become unsafe if they attract bees and offer nowhere to land. Small design details-stones in a water dish, protected soil and varied plant height-can influence whether a site is usable.

Bees navigate using landmarks, odours and the sun's position as a navigation compass. A worker may travel several hundred metres from a nest, which means one garden's insects can be connected to other sites. This connectivity is important when small habitat patches are separated by roads and buildings.

Food is not the only requirement. Many solitary bees nest in bare soil, hollow stems or old masonry. In some districts, a lack of nesting sites is more serious than a lack of flowers. A garden with abundant blooms may still support few bees if suitable nesting material is absent.

Pesticides create another risk. Exposure can kill insects directly, but lower doses may affect a bee's ability to navigate or learn the location of food. Gardeners therefore need to consider timing, application method and whether a treatment is necessary.

Researchers count bees along fixed transects and at flowers. A single garden count tells us which insects appear there, but it cannot show movement between sites. Mark-and-recapture studies use tiny tags or paint marks to identify individuals, although these methods are more demanding.

Rooftop gardens can help, especially where ground-level land is scarce, but they do not replace every habitat. Their value increases when they form a connected network. Plant choice should consider native status, flowering time, nectar quality, water needs and maintenance. Native plants are often valuable, but "native" alone does not guarantee food throughout the year.

The practical conclusion is that urban bee policy should combine habitat creation, careful management and monitoring. A city does not need to select one ideal bee. It needs a mosaic of places in which different species can feed, nest and move safely.

parts.title: Passage 1
parts.passage:
[1] Urban trees are often valued for beauty, but their practical functions are increasingly central to city planning. A canopy shades pavement, leaves intercept rainfall and roots can help soil absorb water. Trees also provide habitat and may reduce the psychological stress associated with traffic. These benefits are real, but they are not automatic. A tree planted in a small, compacted pit may survive poorly, create pavement damage or require more water than a city can supply.

[2] The cooling effect depends on species, canopy size and local form. A mature tree can block solar radiation that would otherwise heat a wall or road. Through transpiration, it transfers water to the atmosphere, although this process slows during drought. A line of trees may cool a footpath while trapping warm air in a narrow street. Planners therefore need information about wind as well as shade.

[3] Rainfall management is another benefit. Leaves and branches delay the moment when rain reaches the ground, and roots create channels through soil. During a short storm, this can reduce the pressure on drains. Trees cannot absorb an unlimited downpour, however. Their contribution is greatest when combined with permeable surfaces, rain gardens and storage basins.

[4] The choice of species involves trade-offs. Fast-growing trees provide canopy quickly but may have weak wood or high water demands. Some species tolerate pollution but support fewer insects. A tree that is appropriate in one climate may become invasive or vulnerable in another. Diversity is recommended because a street planted with one species can suffer widespread loss if a pest arrives.

[5] Maintenance determines whether promised benefits last. Young trees need watering and protection from vehicles. Mature trees require inspection, pruning and sufficient root space. Budgets often favour planting ceremonies rather than years of care, yet the largest cooling and habitat benefits arrive after the initial project has ended. Cities that count only trees planted may exaggerate success.

[6] Equity is an important consideration. Wealthier districts frequently have older, larger canopies, while industrial or lower-income neighbourhoods may have wide areas of exposed pavement. Planting programmes that follow complaints or property value can widen the difference. A fair strategy maps heat, health vulnerability and existing canopy, then directs resources towards places with the greatest need.

[7] Residents can help trees succeed, but community enthusiasm is not a substitute for professional planning. People may water a young tree, report damage or protect a planting site. They may also object when roots lift pavements or branches block signs. Clear responsibility for maintenance and communication about expected changes reduce conflict.

[8] Trees can be part of a stormwater network, but their roots need room to perform that role. Narrow planting pits force roots into compacted soil and may direct them towards pipes or foundations. Structural soil, suspended pavements and connected planting beds give roots more space while allowing pedestrians to use the surface. These systems cost more at the beginning, yet they may reduce repairs and allow a tree to reach the size at which its benefits become substantial.

[9] Urban forestry must also respond to emergencies. During a heatwave, a newly planted tree cannot provide the shade of an established canopy, so cities may need temporary shelters and welfare checks as well. After a storm, damaged branches must be removed safely, but excessive pruning can weaken the tree. A resilient programme plans for these periods instead of evaluating trees only in ordinary weather.

[10] The question of value is therefore longer term than a single budget year. A tree may appear expensive when judged by planting cost and immediate maintenance, but its benefits accumulate through cooler routes, reduced runoff, habitat and social use. Good accounting makes both the investment and the distribution of benefits visible.

[11] Urban forestry is consequently a long-term infrastructure programme. It should be designed with drainage, transport, housing and public health rather than added as decoration. The best projects combine the right tree in the right place with enough soil, water, maintenance and social consent to let the tree become useful.

[12] Evaluation should follow the same long horizon. Canopy surveys can show whether planting has increased shade, while temperature and runoff measurements indicate whether the expected services are occurring. Interviews may reveal that a technically successful project has made a route harder to cross or has displaced a familiar gathering place. A city that revisits its assumptions can improve later planting rather than treating the first plan as final.

[13] The benefits may also cross administrative boundaries. A tree planted beside a school can cool a street managed by another department, and a connected drainage bed can reduce pressure on a downstream district. Shared benefits make shared budgets worthwhile, but they also make accountability harder. Agreements should state who waters, prunes, repairs and evaluates the planting so that success is not claimed by one agency while costs are left to another.

[14] Species choice should reflect the people who use the street as well as the climate. A canopy that blocks a shop sign may affect a small business, while fruit dropping on a pavement may create a slipping risk. These are manageable issues, not reasons to reject planting, but they should be considered during design. Practical consultation can turn objections into adjustments before the tree is in the ground.

parts.title: Passage 2
parts.passage:
[1] For generations, museums were judged chiefly by the quality and rarity of the objects they displayed. A collection of paintings, fossils or tools was arranged behind labels, and visitors were expected to look carefully and learn. Contemporary museums still depend on objects, but many now define their role more broadly. They collect memories, sounds, community knowledge and digital records, and they ask who has the authority to explain an object's meaning.

[2] This change is partly a response to criticism. Traditional displays often presented one institutional story while treating the people connected with an object as background. A ceremonial item might be described through its material and date but not through the community's rules about who may view it. A museum can be legally entitled to hold an object and still face a moral question about whether it should display, return or restrict it.

[3] Community collaboration offers one approach. Museums invite residents to identify people in photographs, record oral histories or advise on exhibition language. Such projects can correct errors and reveal interpretations absent from catalogues. They also require time. A community is not a single voice, and disagreement may be a valuable part of the record rather than a problem to be edited away.

[4] Digital technology expands access but introduces its own inequalities. A three-dimensional scan can let a researcher examine an object without handling it, and an online catalogue can reach people far from the museum. Yet high-speed internet, language access and disability-friendly design are uneven. Digitizing an object does not necessarily make it accessible, and a digital copy may not carry the cultural permissions attached to the original.

[5] Museums also face the problem of scale. They can collect almost unlimited digital files, but storage, preservation and description require resources. A photograph saved today may be unreadable in twenty years if its format or software disappears. Selection remains necessary, even when the material appears abundant. Curators must decide what future researchers may need, while acknowledging that present priorities shape the archive.

[6] The visitor experience is changing as well. Interactive displays can invite questions and multiple interpretations, but interactivity is not automatically educational. Touchscreens may distract from an object, and a dramatic reconstruction can blur the difference between evidence and imagination. Good design makes the status of information clear and allows visitors to pause, compare and disagree.

[7] Questions of return and repair are becoming more visible alongside display. A museum may hold an object acquired under colonial conditions, or a recording made when a community had little power to negotiate its use. Returning an item is one possible response, but so are shared guardianship, restricted access and collaborative interpretation. The appropriate decision depends on the object, the community and the legal history; there is no single gesture that resolves every case.

[8] Climate control creates a practical tension. Stable temperature and humidity protect many collections, but heating and cooling consume energy. Museums are testing lower-energy storage, passive ventilation and more selective display conditions. Preservation standards must remain evidence-based, because a small change may be harmless for one material and damaging for another. Environmental responsibility therefore requires knowledge of the collection rather than a universal thermostat setting.

[9] Staff skills are changing too. A curator may work with a software specialist, a community facilitator, an access adviser and a conservator. Collaboration can broaden what the museum does, but it also requires time for training and decision-making. If institutions add digital and participatory work without funding the people who maintain it, the new model will become another promise that the collection cannot sustain.

[10] The museum's public value is increasingly measured by relationships rather than attendance alone. A smaller exhibition may build trust with a community, support school learning or return knowledge to its source. These outcomes are difficult to summarize in one number, which creates tension with funding systems that prefer simple metrics. Museums need evidence of reach, but they also need language for depth and responsibility.

[11] The museum of the future will not abandon collections. It will make the decisions behind them more visible: who selected an object, whose voice is missing, what restrictions apply and how a record can be challenged. The institution remains a place of preservation, but preservation is linked to care, consent and continuing conversation.

[12] This model changes the meaning of expertise. Conservation science remains essential, but it is joined by language knowledge, community history, disability access and digital preservation. No single curator can possess all of these skills. Museums that share authority may make decisions more slowly, yet the resulting records can be more accurate and more trusted. The cost of consultation is part of responsible stewardship, not an optional extra added after an exhibition is planned.

[13] Visitors should be told when an exhibition contains uncertainty. A label can distinguish a documented fact from a plausible reconstruction, and a catalogue can record disagreement rather than hiding it. This does not make the museum less authoritative. It shows how knowledge was assembled and gives visitors a chance to understand why an interpretation may change as new evidence or community guidance becomes available.

[14] Access includes the right to encounter an object in more than one way. Captions, tactile models, audio description and quiet hours can make a display useful to people who cannot rely on a standard visual visit. These features are not merely accommodations added for a small minority; they often improve clarity for everyone by making the structure of an exhibit explicit.

parts.title: Passage 3
parts.passage:
[1] Migration is often explained through a simple contrast between "push" and "pull" factors. War, unemployment or environmental damage push people away, while jobs, safety or family networks pull them towards a destination. The contrast is useful as a starting point, but it can hide the decisions and constraints between origin and destination. People may move because a relative has gone first, because transport has become affordable or because staying has become less secure without becoming impossible.

[2] Migration decisions are made within households as well as by individuals. One member may move to earn money, while others remain to care for children or older relatives. Remittances can support education, housing and healthcare, but the absence of a worker may increase the unpaid labour carried by those who stay. A household can therefore experience migration as both an opportunity and a burden.

[3] Networks influence destinations. A person who knows someone in another city has information about jobs, accommodation and routes, reducing the uncertainty of travel. Networks can also narrow choices. New arrivals may enter the same occupation as relatives because it is accessible, even when their qualifications would suit other work. Over time, a network may become a bridge to opportunity or a channel into dependence.

[4] Policy categories do not always match lived experience. A person may move because crops fail, but may not qualify for a legal category designed for persecution. Another may cross a border temporarily, return several times and still be counted as a permanent migrant in one dataset. Definitions affect rights, statistics and public narratives. They are not merely labels applied after the event.

[5] Environmental change illustrates the problem of single-cause explanations. Flooding or drought can reduce income, but households may respond by changing crops, selling assets or sending one member elsewhere. Migration may be a strategy of adaptation rather than a final escape. In other cases, environmental stress makes movement impossible because people lack money, documents or transport. The same hazard can produce mobility in one group and immobility in another.

[6] Cities receive migrants unevenly. New arrivals may settle where rents are low and networks exist, which can produce concentrated communities. Concentration can support shops, language services and mutual aid, but it may also expose residents to overcrowding or discrimination. A policy that disperses migrants in the name of integration can weaken the networks that make employment and childcare possible.

[7] Public debate often treats numbers as if they described experience. A rising migration total does not show why people moved, what resources they used or whether they intend to stay. Qualitative interviews and longitudinal research can reveal change over time, although they are more expensive than a one-time count. Combining methods is not an optional luxury when the process itself is changing.

[8] Gender and age can shape the meaning of a move. A young adult may migrate for study and later sponsor relatives, while an older person may move in the opposite direction to provide care. Women may enter paid work after migration but continue to carry domestic responsibilities across borders. These patterns are easily missed when the migrant is represented as a single wage earner.

[9] Remittances also have a social geography. Money sent home can improve a family's housing or education, but it may create expectations that the migrant must continue sending funds even during unemployment. Communities may become dependent on transfers while local public services remain weak. Research should therefore ask not only how much money moves, but who controls it and what opportunities it creates.

[10] Return is not always the end of migration. People may circulate between places, keep businesses in two regions or return with new skills that are difficult to use in the local economy. A policy focused on permanent settlement can overlook these repeated movements. Longitudinal studies are useful because they show that a person's category can change as circumstances change.

[11] The most useful account of migration is therefore relational. It considers household strategies, social networks, law, markets and environmental conditions together. People do make choices, but choices are distributed unequally. Understanding movement requires attention both to motivation and to the resources that make one option possible and another unrealistic.

[12] This perspective also improves public debate. Instead of asking whether migration is simply good or bad, policy-makers can ask which rights, services and labour markets are affected in a particular place. A town receiving seasonal workers may need housing and transport at one time of year, while a city receiving students may need language support and recognition of qualifications. Specific questions lead to more practical responses than a single national number.

[13] It also discourages the assumption that movement is a one-way process. People maintain ties through visits, money, phone calls and political participation, and these connections can influence both the place of departure and the place of arrival. A migration policy that considers only the border crossing may miss the institutions and relationships that make the movement sustainable.

[14] The language used by authorities can influence those relationships. Describing a group only as a burden may encourage exclusion, while describing every movement as an economic gain can hide insecurity. Careful categories and evidence do not remove political disagreement, but they make it harder for a slogan to stand in for the varied experiences of migrants and residents.

parts.transcript:
Receptionist: Good afternoon, Maple Leaf Hostel. How can I help?

Lena: I'd like to book a bed for a week. The name is O'Connor.

Receptionist: We have beds from 12 to 20 August, which is eight nights if you arrive on the 12th and leave on the 20th.

Lena: I only need seven nights, so I'll leave on the 19th.

Receptionist: Fine. Would you like the mixed dormitory or the female dormitory?

Lena: Female, please. Is the address easy to find?

Receptionist: We're at 28 Willow Street, opposite the post office. At check-in, guests receive a free map of the old town.

Lena: Is there a kitchen for guests who do not want the set breakfast?

Receptionist: Yes, the shared kitchen is beside the courtyard. It has two fridges, and each bed has a numbered shelf. Please label food with your departure date; anything left behind is cleared every morning. The kitchen closes for cleaning between two and three in the afternoon.

Lena: I'll be arriving by train. Is the hostel far from the station?

Receptionist: About fifteen minutes on foot, or five minutes by tram. The tram stop is on the other side of the post office. If you arrive after midnight, use the night entrance and ring the bell rather than trying the daytime door.

Lena: Does breakfast take place downstairs?

Receptionist: It's served in the courtyard from seven until ten. The kitchen is inside, but guests eat outdoors in good weather.

Lena: I have a knee problem. Could I have a lower bunk?

Receptionist: Certainly. I'll request a lower bunk. We can't guarantee a particular bed until arrival, but we'll try.

Lena: What are the quiet hours?

Receptionist: They begin at 11 p.m. Please keep music and calls low after that.

Lena: And the deposit?

Receptionist: It's 30 euros, paid in cash on arrival and returned when the key is handed back.

parts.transcript:
This announcement concerns the new Route 42 bus service. It was introduced to connect the northern housing area with the rest of the city, not primarily to serve the airport or the hospital. The first month is a trial, and passengers can use the route with a reduced ticket. Normal fares will apply after the trial unless the council changes the plan.

The busiest stop is expected to be Central Library, where the route meets two other services. Hill Market is popular on Saturdays, while Riverside Station has more passengers in the morning.

Because roadworks are taking place beside the library, buses after 8 p.m. will stop on the opposite side of the street. The change is temporary and will be signed clearly. It does not affect daytime buses.

Passengers with bicycles should use the rear door, where the rack is located. The driver may refuse a bicycle if the rack is full, but folding bicycles can be carried if they are safely stored.

The first weekday bus leaves at 5:40 a.m. The electronic timetable at each stop is updated every five minutes. The passenger app shows the bus's current location, although the information may be delayed in poor network conditions.

The trial will also collect information about reliability. Inspectors will record whether buses leave on time and whether the full route is completed. A delay caused by roadworks will be logged differently from a delay caused by a vehicle fault, because the council needs to know which problem the service can control. Passengers can still report crowding, but a complaint does not automatically mean that an additional bus will be added.

The council wants comments on the trial. Send them by email using the address on the timetable, rather than giving them to the driver, who cannot record detailed feedback while working.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.instructions: Play the synthetic recording once. Read the question limits carefully before you begin.
parts.transcript:
Adviser: I've read your proposal on engagement in online courses. You currently measure engagement by the number of log-ins.

Sara: It seemed objective.

Adviser: It is easy to count, but a log-in does not show whether a student understood the material. Someone may open the platform briefly, while another downloads a file and studies offline.

Amir: We could also count attendance at live seminars.

Adviser: Include it as one indicator, not as the definition. Students may have caring responsibilities or work at those times.

Sara: We want to interview students about their experience.

Adviser: Good. The interviews should explore why students use or avoid parts of the platform. Ask about weekly instructions and assessment deadlines. Internet access at home may also explain patterns, so include that. Favourite social-media platforms and family history are outside your question.

Amir: Our sample comes from the first-year economics course. Is that acceptable?

Adviser: It is manageable, but say that your findings are course-specific. Your larger problem is that you selected only active students. Those who withdrew are missing, yet their experience may explain disengagement.

Sara: Some students also watch the lecture at double speed. The platform records that as a shorter session, even though they may have watched all the material.

Adviser: That is a good example of why platform activity is not identical to learning. Record it as a possible pattern, but do not assume that faster playback means better or worse engagement. Ask participants how they use the feature and what they do afterwards.

Amir: We should probably distinguish compulsory activities from optional discussion boards.

Adviser: Yes. Course design determines what a log-in means. A student may be active because a quiz is required, or because a discussion genuinely helps them. Your interview guide should leave room for both explanations.

Sara: We can invite withdrawn students if we have their contact details.

Adviser: Try, and explain the ethical procedure. Do not pressure them to participate.

Amir: Should we treat engagement as a personality trait? Some people are naturally organised.

Adviser: That is too fixed. Present it as a changing relationship with course design, time, support and personal circumstances. Technology is part of the setting, not the only cause.

Sara: How many pilot interviews do we need?

Adviser: Six students should reveal whether the questions are understandable. Then revise the guide before the main sample.

Amir: We'll code answers by theme.

Adviser: Send me the coding scheme before the end of October. If you wait until all interviews are finished, you may discover that important information was never collected.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.instructions: Play the synthetic recording once. Read the question limits carefully before you begin.
parts.transcript:
Today's lecture examines memory and learning. Working memory temporarily holds information for active processing. It is not a general measure of intelligence; it is a limited workspace. If a learner tries to keep a long list of unfamiliar terms in mind while solving a problem, the system can become overloaded.

One way to reduce overload is to group information into meaningful units. A long sequence of letters may be difficult when treated separately, but familiar words can be handled as larger chunks. Prior knowledge therefore changes the apparent difficulty of a task. What is heavy for a beginner may be manageable for an expert because the expert has more useful structures already stored in long-term memory.

Learning also involves long-term memory. New information becomes more stable through consolidation, a process influenced by practice and sleep. Consolidation does not mean that every detail is preserved exactly. Memories are reconstructed, which is one reason explanation and application are important.

A common study habit is rereading. Rereading can create a feeling of familiarity, but retrieval practice is often stronger. It asks the learner to recall information without looking at the page, then check the answer. The effort is a desirable difficulty: the task feels harder, but the effort can strengthen later recall. Difficulty is useful only when it remains manageable and feedback is available.

Feedback should be specific enough to guide another attempt. A numerical grade may show how well a learner performed overall, but "six out of ten" does not explain which idea was misunderstood. A comment identifying the error and suggesting the next step turns assessment into information.

Feedback timing depends on the task. Immediate correction can prevent a basic misconception from becoming familiar, while a short delay may encourage a learner to examine an answer independently. In either case, the learner needs an opportunity to try again. Feedback that arrives after the final assessment may be accurate but has little power to improve the performance that produced it.

Sleep contributes to learning by helping the brain reorganise memories. It is not a substitute for study, and an exhausted learner may not encode information effectively in the first place. Short breaks can also protect attention during practice.

One effective schedule uses spaced retrieval. Instead of studying a topic once for three hours, the learner returns to it over several days and attempts to recall the key ideas. The intervals can expand as recall becomes easier. Practice questions, explanation to another person and mixed problem types all require active use.

The final message is simple but not effortless: combine retrieval practice with regular sleep, feedback and deliberate review. Avoiding every difficult task produces confidence without durable learning, while making every task impossible produces frustration. The aim is a sequence of challenges that the learner can meet with support.

parts.title: Passage 1
parts.passage:
[1] Concrete is one of the most widely used materials in the world, and its production has a large environmental footprint. Cement manufacture releases carbon dioxide through fuel use and the chemical transformation of limestone. At the same time, cities demolish buildings and produce enormous quantities of rubble. Recycled concrete aggregate-crushed material recovered from old structures-appears to offer a way to reduce both landfill and demand for newly quarried stone.

[2] The process begins with sorting. Reinforcing steel, wood, glass and plaster must be removed before concrete is crushed. The resulting particles vary in size and may contain old mortar attached to the original stone. That attached mortar makes recycled aggregate more porous than new aggregate. It can absorb more water, affect workability and reduce the predictability of a fresh mixture.

[3] Engineers can adjust the mixture. They may pre-soak recycled particles, add water-reducing agents or combine recycled aggregate with a proportion of new material. The correct approach depends on the intended use. Concrete for a structural column faces different requirements from concrete used beneath a pavement or in a non-load-bearing wall. "Recycled" is therefore not a single performance category.

[4] Testing is essential. Compressive strength, absorption, shrinkage and resistance to repeated freezing can vary according to the source building and crushing method. A batch from a well-documented demolition site may be more reliable than a mixed load from several unknown sources. Quality control can raise costs, but without it a designer may compensate by using more cement, reducing some of the environmental benefit.

[5] The carbon calculation is also more complex than it first appears. Reusing material near the demolition site may avoid quarrying and long-distance transport. Processing requires electricity, and transporting heavy aggregate to a new project can erase the saving. A local project with a moderate recycled content may be better than a distant project with a higher percentage.

[6] Building regulations have traditionally favoured conservative assumptions. Designers may hesitate to specify recycled aggregate if approval procedures are unclear or if insurance companies regard it as unusual. Demonstration projects and updated standards can reduce this barrier, but engineers still need evidence that local material streams are consistent.

[7] Some projects use a material passport: a record of where components came from, how they were processed and how they might be recovered in the future. Such records can improve confidence when a building is altered or demolished again. They are most useful when information is collected during construction rather than reconstructed years later from incomplete invoices. A passport cannot guarantee reuse, but it makes the next decision less dependent on guesswork.

[8] Designers also distinguish between downcycling and keeping performance. Crushed concrete used as road base may be an excellent use of material even if it does not return to a structural frame. The aim should be to match the recovered material to a safe, valuable application, not to force every component into its original role. In some cases, direct reuse of a wall panel or beam avoids crushing altogether and preserves more of the energy already invested.

[9] The economics change as demolition becomes more selective. Separating material at a site takes labour and time, but mixed waste can attract disposal fees and lose resale value. Contracts that reward recovery, rather than paying only for rapid clearance, can change behaviour. This is an example of how environmental performance depends on procurement as well as engineering.

[10] Recycling does not remove the need to reduce new construction. A building that remains in use generally avoids more emissions than one demolished and replaced with a partly recycled structure. Design for adaptation, repair and long life therefore comes first. When demolition is unavoidable, careful recovery can keep material in circulation rather than treating it as waste.

[11] The future of concrete is likely to involve several strategies: lower-carbon cement, more efficient structures, reuse of existing buildings and selective use of recycled aggregate. No single percentage makes a project sustainable. The meaningful question is whether material, energy, transport and service life have been considered together.

[12] This broader view changes what counts as a successful demolition. A contractor may be praised for recovering a large mass of aggregate, even when valuable doors, tiles or structural elements were discarded because they required careful removal. Conversely, a project with a smaller recycled percentage may preserve more components for direct reuse. Assessment should record the quality and future use of recovered material, not merely its weight.

[13] Public procurement can encourage these distinctions. A contract may specify recycled content, but it can also require evidence of local sourcing, recovery rates and future disassembly. Such requirements give suppliers a reason to invest in sorting and documentation. They also prevent sustainability from becoming a single number that looks impressive while leaving transport, waste and durability outside the calculation.

[14] Consumers rarely see these choices directly. A building may advertise recycled content without explaining the source, processing energy or expected service life. Clear reporting would allow clients to compare projects on more than a headline percentage. It would also reward firms that invest in reliable local recovery systems instead of treating recycled aggregate as an occasional marketing feature.

parts.title: Passage 2
parts.passage:
[1] The term "blue zone" is used for places where researchers have reported unusually high numbers of people living to advanced ages. Popular accounts often present these places as proof that one diet or one daily ritual produces longevity. The research is more cautious. Long life reflects interacting influences, including genes, income, medical care, social connection, physical activity and the accuracy of records.

[2] Demography is difficult at extreme ages. Birth registration may have been incomplete, names may change, and family stories can be repeated as evidence. Researchers therefore compare official documents, census records and sometimes historical events remembered by the individual. A place should not be called a blue zone solely because it contains several famous older residents.

[3] Lifestyle patterns nevertheless offer useful clues. In several long-lived communities, people move as part of ordinary work rather than following a separate exercise programme. They may walk to neighbours, tend gardens or use stairs. These activities are moderate but repeated. The lesson is not that strenuous sport is unnecessary for everyone; it is that movement can be built into the environment and routine.

[4] Food is another area of interest. Traditional diets in some regions include beans, whole grains, vegetables and modest amounts of animal products. Yet diets change over time, and visitors may eat differently from older residents. A food list cannot explain longevity without considering portion size, processing, income and the wider pattern of meals.

[5] Social connection is often prominent in the research. Older adults may live near relatives, belong to mutual-aid groups or hold valued responsibilities. Social ties can provide emotional support and practical help, but they can also create obligations and stress. Researchers should avoid turning a complex social system into a prescription that every person must copy.

[6] Purpose is sometimes described as a psychological ingredient. Having a reason to get up may encourage activity and social contact, while social roles can give a person's knowledge a place in the community. Measuring purpose is difficult, however. A questionnaire response reflects language, culture and the moment at which it is answered.

[7] Medical care and public infrastructure should not be ignored. Clean water, safe roads, vaccination, accessible clinics and stable housing shape whether healthy habits are possible. A community may appear to benefit from a cultural tradition when it also benefits from an unusually supportive environment. The most attractive explanation is not always the most complete.

[8] Selection effects are another concern. People who reach an advanced age may have survived earlier illness, maintained strong social ties or possessed resources that were not available to everyone in their generation. Studying survivors can reveal protective factors, but it can also make a behaviour seem more powerful than it was for people who did not survive. Comparisons with less long-lived groups and with earlier generations are needed to separate association from cause.

[9] Genetic variation may influence ageing, but genes interact with surroundings. A trait that is helpful in one food system or climate may have little effect elsewhere. This is why researchers are cautious about turning a community finding into a commercial genetic test. Healthy ageing is not a single biological pathway, and a statistical association does not tell an individual what will happen.

[10] Public policy can learn from blue-zone research without copying it literally. Cities might invest in safe walking routes, social centres and affordable fresh food rather than telling residents to imitate another culture's menu. These changes improve the conditions in which healthy choices are possible. They also benefit people who will never live to an extreme age, which is a more defensible public-health goal.

[11] Blue-zone research is valuable when it generates questions rather than rigid rules. It suggests that long-term health is embedded in relationships, food systems, movement and public conditions. It does not justify selling a supplement, copying another culture's menu or claiming that an individual is responsible for every aspect of ageing. The evidence is strongest when social context remains visible.

[12] The language of exceptional longevity can also affect how older people are treated. If a community is presented as naturally healthy, its residents may be expected to remain active and cheerful even when they need care. A better interpretation recognizes both capability and vulnerability. The point of studying long lives is not to deny illness or prescribe endless productivity, but to understand which social arrangements help people maintain choice and connection as their circumstances change.

[13] Researchers should also be careful about survivor stories. An individual who attributes a long life to one habit may be sincere, but personal explanation is not the same as comparative evidence. Memory selects memorable routines and may overlook ordinary advantages such as stable housing or a supportive family. Interviews are valuable for understanding meaning; they become stronger when combined with demographic and health records.

[14] Ageing research also needs a realistic definition of success. More years are not the only outcome; independence, relief from pain, participation and the ability to make decisions matter as well. A policy that increases lifespan but leaves people isolated may not reflect the values that older residents themselves describe. Listening to those residents is part of interpreting the evidence.

parts.title: Passage 3
parts.passage:
[1] Digitization is often described as preservation: a fragile manuscript is scanned, a tape is converted into a file, and a photograph is stored in several locations. The process can protect information from physical decay and make a collection available to researchers who cannot visit. Yet a digital archive is not a transparent window onto the past. Decisions about selection, description, format and access shape what future users will be able to find and understand.

[2] Selection begins with the original collection. No archive can preserve everything, and digitization usually favours material that is popular, physically manageable or funded by a particular project. A box that remains unscanned has not disappeared, but it may become invisible to users who search only online. The absence of a digital record can therefore be mistaken for the absence of historical evidence.

[3] Description creates another layer. A file may be labelled with a date, place and subject, but such labels reflect the vocabulary of the institution. A photograph described as "factory workers" may have been identified by a curator who did not know the people's names. Community tagging can add detail, although user-generated descriptions require moderation and may conflict. Multiple labels may be more honest than one authoritative phrase.

[4] Formats affect access and survival. A high-resolution image requires more storage but may support analysis of texture or handwriting. Compression makes files easier to deliver but can remove information. Audio digitization involves choices about sampling and noise reduction. The "best" format depends on the purpose, and an archive may retain a preservation master while creating smaller access copies.

[5] Storage is not permanence. Files need checks for corruption, migration to new systems and documentation of the software required to interpret them. Cloud storage can provide geographic redundancy, but it depends on contracts, energy and continued payment. A small institution may prefer local copies under its control, while a larger network can distribute responsibility across several repositories.

[6] Access presents an ethical tension. Digitizing a collection can return materials to communities, but it can also expose personal information or sacred knowledge. Some archives use layered access, allowing the public to see a description while restricting the file itself. Consent may need to be revisited because a recording created for a local project can acquire a global audience when placed online.

[7] Search systems influence memory. A user who receives results ranked by popularity may encounter the most frequently described material rather than the most representative. Automated transcription can make a collection searchable, but errors may be concentrated in unfamiliar accents or languages. Researchers should treat search results as a route into the archive, not as a neutral map of everything that exists.

[8] Version control is particularly important for born-digital records. A website, database or social-media feed may change every day, and a saved copy without a date or capture method can be difficult to interpret. Archives may preserve several versions, but doing so raises questions about personal information, platform terms and whether a person expected a temporary post to become permanent evidence. Description should record these conditions rather than pretending that the file is a complete original.

[9] Metadata can also be contested. A place name may have an official spelling, a local spelling and a name used before a political change. Search systems that accept only one form can hide relevant records. Including alternative terms, relationships and community-preferred names improves discovery, but it requires institutions to acknowledge that description is an act of interpretation.

[10] Community governance offers a way to address some of these issues. A local group may decide that a record can be viewed by residents but not downloaded, or that a sacred name should not be indexed publicly. Such rules can complicate the dream of universal access, yet access without permission can reproduce the harm that preservation was meant to prevent. A trustworthy archive explains its restrictions and provides a route for future review.

[11] Digital preservation is consequently a social practice. It requires technical maintenance, but also decisions about whose records are selected, how names are used and who may enter. The goal is not to create a perfect copy of the past. It is to build a trustworthy, revisable pathway through evidence, with enough documentation for future users to understand both the records and the choices that shaped them.

[12] Revisability is essential because archives acquire new meanings. A description that seemed harmless may later be recognized as insulting, incomplete or legally inaccurate. Changing the label should not erase the earlier record; the archive can preserve a history of description and explain why an update was made. This approach treats correction as part of preservation rather than as a threat to institutional authority.

[13] Future users may also need to know what was not preserved. A project can document discarded duplicates, unreadable formats, missing pages and restrictions on access. This negative information prevents later researchers from assuming that a quiet search result represents a complete collection. It also gives communities a basis for deciding whether a missing item should be sought elsewhere or whether a gap should remain respected.

[14] The archive must preserve its own operating history too. Future researchers may need to know when a migration changed file names, when a transcription engine was replaced or when an access rule was revised. Such records are not glamorous, but they allow users to distinguish a change in the historical material from a change introduced by the archive itself.

RACHEL: Oh, hi. I'm calling about the adult swimming club - I saw a poster in the gym last week.

RACHEL: Yes, of course.
STAFF: Great, can I get your full name first?
RACHEL: It's Rachel Fenwick. F-E-N-W-I-C-K.
STAFF: Thanks. And a contact number?
RACHEL: 0798 226 4471.
STAFF: Perfect. Now, the club actually runs two sessions - Tuesday evenings and, um, I thought it was Thursday mornings, but actually that one's been changed to Saturday mornings, sorry.

parts.transcript: Good evening, everyone, and thanks for coming along. I'm here to tell you about the Brookfield Community Garden, which opens to the public next month. The garden covers just over two acres of what used to be an unused car park behind the old railway station. We've divided it into four main zones. The first, nearest the entrance, is the Herb and Vegetable Zone, where local residents can rent individual plots. Next to that is the Wildflower Meadow, which we've deliberately left unmanicured to attract pollinators like bees and butterflies. Beyond that is the Children's Zone, with a small maze and a sensory garden designed for younger visitors. And finally, at the far end near the old station wall, is the Quiet Garden, a space with benches and shade trees for relaxation. If you'd like to rent a vegetable plot, applications open on the first of next month, and priority will be given to residents living within half a mile of the garden. The rental fee is twenty-five pounds per year, which covers water access and a toolshed key. We also run volunteer sessions every Wednesday afternoon from two until four. No experience is necessary - we'll teach you everything from composting to pruning. Volunteers get free seeds each season as a thank-you. One thing I should mention: the garden will be closed to the public on Mondays for maintenance. All other days, opening hours are eight in the morning until sunset. We're also planning a series of workshops. The first, in the autumn, will focus on seed- saving techniques. Later there'll be one on beekeeping basics, though that's still being finalised. A workshop on garden design for small spaces is planned for early winter. Finally, if you're interested in donating tools or equipment, please leave them at the site office rather than at the garden gate, as unattended donations have unfortunately gone missing in the past.

DR AHMADI: So, tell me how the research proposal is coming along.
MARCUS: We've settled on the topic - the effect of noise pollution on urban bird populations - but we're still deciding on methodology.
PRIYA: I wanted to do a purely observational study, just recording bird counts in different areas of the city, but Marcus thinks we need something more controlled.
MARCUS: Right, because without comparing noisy and quiet sites properly, we won't be able to say the differences are actually caused by noise rather than something else - like green space or food availability.
DR AHMADI: That's a fair concern. What sites were you thinking of comparing?
PRIYA: We'd chosen the park next to the ring road, because it's noisy, and Fairview Park, which is quieter. But actually, now I think about it, Fairview also has far more trees, so that's a confounding variable.
DR AHMADI: Exactly the kind of thing you need to control for. Have you thought about using sound-level meters to get objective noise readings, rather than just assuming one site is noisy and another isn't?
MARCUS: We hadn't, actually - that's a good idea. We could take readings at several points across each site.
DR AHMADI: I'd recommend it. It'll also strengthen your data analysis section considerably.
PRIYA: Should we survey local residents too, about how they perceive bird activity?
DR AHMADI: You could, but be careful - perception data is subjective and shouldn't be mixed with your objective bird-count figures without a clear distinction in your write-up.
MARCUS: We were also thinking of doing this over just two weeks.
DR AHMADI: That's quite short for this kind of study. Bird activity can vary a lot with weather and time of day, so I'd suggest extending it, ideally across a full season if your timeline allows.
PRIYA: We do have until the end of the term, so that should be possible.
DR AHMADI: Good. One more thing - make sure you get ethical approval before starting, since you'll be in public parks.
MARCUS: We've already submitted the ethics form, actually.
DR AHMADI: Excellent, that's ahead of schedule. Let's meet again in two weeks to review your first data.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.instructions: Play the synthetic recording once. Read the question limits carefully before you begin.
parts.transcript: Today I want to look at how the design of public libraries has changed since the nineteenth century, and what that tells us about how societies value shared knowledge. The earliest public libraries in the industrial era were often built to resemble temples or grand civic buildings - think tall columns, marble staircases, high ceilings. The intention was to inspire a sense of awe and to signal that reading was a serious, almost sacred, civic activity. However, this design had a drawback: these buildings could feel intimidating, particularly to working-class visitors who weren't accustomed to such formal spaces. By the mid-twentieth century, library design shifted noticeably. Architects began favouring open-plan layouts, natural lighting, and lower, more approachable shelving. The goal was accessibility rather than grandeur. This period also introduced the idea of the library as a community hub - not just a place to borrow books, but somewhere people might attend a lecture, join a reading group, or simply sit and read a newspaper. An interesting turning point came in the 1970s and 80s with the introduction of computer catalogues, which eventually replaced the traditional card index. This freed up significant floor space that had previously been devoted to filing cabinets, and much of that space was reinstated as public seating or children's areas. More recently, the rise of digital media has forced libraries to reconsider their purpose entirely. Many modern libraries now dedicate considerable space to technology - computer labs, recording studios, even spaces for 3D printing. Some critics have argued this risks diluting the library's core identity, though others see it as a natural evolution, keeping the institution relevant to contemporary needs. One particularly notable modern trend is the "library as living room" concept, where comfortable seating, cafés, and flexible furniture aim to make the space feel less institutional and more like an extension of people's homes. Proponents argue this increases visit frequency, especially among younger people who might otherwise never set foot in a library. There are also environmental considerations shaping contemporary library architecture. New builds increasingly incorporate green roofs, natural ventilation systems, and materials with lower carbon footprints, partly in response to public funding bodies now requiring sustainability credentials for new civic buildings. Finally, I want to mention the ongoing debate around silence. Traditionally, libraries enforced strict silence, but many modern libraries now designate specific quiet zones while allowing conversation and group work elsewhere. This division attempts to serve both traditional readers and a newer generation of visitors who use libraries as collaborative workspaces.

parts.title: Passage 1
parts.passage:
[1] For nearly four centuries, the European beaver (Castor fiber) was absent from much of Britain, hunted to extinction for its fur, meat, and a glandular secretion once used in medicine and perfume. Yet in recent decades, this large semi-aquatic rodent has staged a remarkable comeback, reintroduced first through licensed trial programmes and now, in some regions, allowed to spread freely across river catchments.

[2] Beavers are often described by ecologists as a "keystone species," meaning their presence has effects on the environment far beyond their own population. The most visible of these effects is dam-building. Using branches, mud, and stones, beavers construct dams across streams to raise water levels, creating ponds that offer them protection from predators and easier access to food during winter. These engineered wetlands, however, do far more than serve the beavers themselves. Slower-moving water allows sediment to settle, improving water clarity downstream, while the wetland margins created by flooding become rich habitats for insects, amphibians, and wading birds.

[3] One of the most cited benefits of beaver reintroduction is flood mitigation. Dams slow the flow of water during heavy rainfall, reducing peak flood volumes further downstream. A widely referenced study of a beaver-modified site in Devon found that water leaving the site during storm events was released more slowly and over a longer period than water entering it, easing pressure on flood-prone areas nearby. This has led some conservation groups to advocate for beaver reintroduction as a low-cost, natural alternative to engineered flood defences.

[4] Not everyone welcomes the beaver's return, however. Farmers, in particular, have raised concerns about dams flooding agricultural land and burrows undermining riverbanks used for irrigation or livestock access. In some cases, beaver activity has felled valuable trees or blocked drainage channels essential for managing farmland. These conflicts have prompted debate over how reintroduction should be managed: should beavers be allowed to spread without restriction, or should their populations and territories be actively controlled? Government and conservation bodies have generally settled on a compromise.

[5] In several regions, licensed "beaver management" schemes now permit selective intervention - for instance, installing devices that prevent dams from raising water to problematic levels, or relocating individual animals from sites where conflict with landowners is severe. Complete removal, once common when beavers caused inconvenience, is now discouraged except as a last resort, reflecting a broader shift in attitude toward coexistence rather than elimination. Scientific interest in beavers has also grown considerably. Researchers studying beaver- engineered wetlands have found that these habitats can support significantly higher biodiversity than comparable areas without beaver activity, with notable increases in aquatic invertebrate and amphibian populations. Some studies further suggest that beaver ponds can improve water quality by trapping agricultural runoff, including excess nutrients that would otherwise contribute to algal blooms downstream - though researchers caution that results vary considerably depending on local geology and land use. Public perception, too, appears to be shifting. Early reintroduction trials were often met with scepticism, partly due to unfamiliarity with a species absent from the landscape for generations, and partly due to genuine concern from rural communities about economic impact. However, surveys conducted in areas with established beaver populations have generally found growing support over time, particularly once residents observe the animals' effects firsthand rather than relying on assumptions. Ecotourism has also emerged as an unexpected economic benefit in some areas, with visitors travelling specifically to observe wild beavers or their engineering works.

[6] Looking ahead, the question is less whether beavers will remain part of Britain's landscape - their populations continue to expand steadily - and more how their presence will be managed as they inevitably come into greater contact with human land use. Advocates argue that with careful, adaptive management, the beaver's return represents one of the more promising examples of a species reintroduction delivering measurable ecological benefit, provided the legitimate concerns of those living alongside them continue to be addressed.
